question: End the scene with lingering sensory details that leave the reader with the feeling of the place.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The travel writer Colin Thubron, in Shadow of the Silk Road, has a lovely way of ending scenes with lingering sensory details and images.

question: End the scene strongly; don’t let it fizzle out.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The ideal is to end a scene strongly; you don’t want it to fizzle out.

question: Leave a scene unresolved when you want suspense or interest to pull readers into the next scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scene endings do not necessarily mean scene resolutions. You may want to leave a scene unresolved in order to create suspense or interest in the next scene.

question: Vary your scene endings—ending every scene with a flourish becomes an obvious device.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Though every single scene doesn’t need to end with a flourish (and frequent use of weighty scene endings can become an obvious device), scenes that end with powerful imagery, dialogue, or action will reverberate in the reader’s mind.

question: Punctuate the scene ending: use it to put form to the scene, emphasize themes, end forward motion, and assert a rest before more scenes and summaries arrive.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Whether you use action, image, or a line of dialogue to end your scene, the ending is a form of punctuation, putting form to the scene, emphasizing themes, ending forward motion, asserting a rest before more scenes and summaries arrive.

question: When a character makes a choice with dramatic import, recast that moment as a scene rather than a summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The writer uses a scene here because this is the moment in which Margaret makes her choice and therefore it has dramatic import.

question: Open a scene in the midst of action or dialogue when you want to cut to the chase and establish the conflict immediately.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Starting in media res works here because it basically cuts to the chase.

question: Where your scene moves at a natural pace, limit the description so it doesn't get bogged down—keep only the details that carry a lot of information about the characters.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you want your scene to give the impression of real time passing at a natural pace, limit the amount of description so the scene doesn't get bogged down but make sure that every bit of description carries a lot of information. Choose your details for what they tell about the characters.

question: Manufacture the time that passes in your scene rather than recording it realistically: select only the actions and thoughts that will have the most impact for your intention.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: So, when you create a scene the passing of time must be represented, it must be manufactured, rather than recorded realistically. You must select the actions and thoughts of the narrator and/or characters within a scene with sensitivity to the choices that will have the most impact, depending on your intention.

question: Work the middle of the scene: intensify conflict, develop and reveal character, and move the action forward as complications arise and the stakes rise.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Once you’ve established reader interest and gotten your scene underway, the middle of the scene is where you intensify conflict, develop and reveal character, and move the action forward. Conflict intensifies as complications arise and the stakes are raised.

question: In a piece carried mostly by summary, stop the ongoing flow of summary and render in scene only the moments of utmost importance to your narrator or protagonist.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The authors have chosen to stop the ongoing flow of summary to focus in closely, through scene, at particular, wellchosen moments that are of utmost importance to the narrator or protagonist.

question: Check that your scene has movement: by its end the reader should feel in a different place—something changed, or the reader’s perception of the characters changed.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When you get to the end of the scene, just as when you get to the end of a book, you want to feel that you are in a different place than when you entered. Within that scene something has changed, or something has changed in your perception of the narrator or characters.

question: Decide how each scene opens—with a slow buildup from the beginning or in medias res—so the choice fits the subject and the mood you want to convey.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: There’s no rule about which way to start a scene—with a slow buildup from the beginning or in medias res—but your choice should fit the nature of the subject and the mood you wish to convey.

question: Write plot-critical events as scenes and summarize the routine ones—match the treatment to the event’s importance.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You want to make sure you use scenes rather than summary whenever you are writing about events that are particularly important to the plot.

question: Decide what you need to reveal about the character in this scene, then articulate the scene’s purpose: what the character wants and what obstacles or aid they will encounter.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can use the interplay between interior thoughts, dialogue, and behavior to establish and reveal character in your own scenes by deciding what you need to show your reader about the character in that particular scene. This means articulating for yourself a purpose for the scene and a purpose for the character in that scene—what your character wants in the scene and what your character will encounter by way of obstacles to that desire (or aid in fulfilling that desire).

question: Check each scene against the jobs scenes perform—emotional connection, dramatized events, plot movement, conflict, suspense, change, character revelation, theme, mood, resolution—and make sure it meets at least a few.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scenes are never there just for “color”; they have several very important jobs to do. Most scenes don’t meet all of the criteria listed below but they should meet at least a few.

question: Establish reader interest quickly in the scene’s opening, whether through immediate conflict or an engaging character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Whether you provide your reader with a slower introduction like Welty or jump right into a scene as Schorer did, it’s important to keep in mind that you need to establish reader interest quickly.

question: To stretch a moment that took only seconds, heighten the character's perception of physical stimuli—what they feel against their skin, what they hear—and let the language grind to a halt.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: His perception of physical stimuli is heightened—he feels the pages of the newspaper rustling against his arm.

question: Open a scene slowly, with scene-setting description first, when the buildup should set the mood and introduce the theme.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The slow buildup sets the appropriate mood and introduces theme (such as Phoenix’s strength against odds).

question: Ask what your adult narrator feels about the younger self in each specific scene—when the younger self was victimized, achieved, or made foolish choices—and let conflicting emotions stand.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: What does the adult narrator feel if her younger self was victimized, if the younger self achieved, if the younger self made foolish choices—be specific, responding to scenes from your story.

question: To speed a scene up, cut sentences into short subject-action constructions and make the verbs explosive and action-filled.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The sentences are short, mostly subject-action constructions, and the verbs are explosive and action-filled.

question: Check where each scene begins: if you start with every preliminary, cut back to the moment that matters so details and irrelevant events don't bury the reader.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You don't want to begin every scene with Adam and Eve or your story would become an unrelenting and oppressive profusion of details and irrelevant events.

question: Audit your draft for the balance of scene and summary: good prose needs both, so find where over-scening or over-summarizing weakens the work.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Good prose almost always requires both showing and telling, scenes and summary, the two basic components of creative prose.

question: Decide passage by passage whether time should be condensed or expanded: use summary to relay many events quickly, a scene to give the impression of real time passing.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: As noted earlier, summary can be used to condense time (in the sense of relaying many events quickly), while a scene expands it (by giving the impression of real time passing).

question: Plant a theme of the larger work early in the scene—even in its first sentence.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Themes of the larger work can be introduced and developed at any point in the scene—beginning, middle, or end.

question: Audit each scene for its three structural parts: a way in (beginning), the work it accomplishes (middle), and a graceful exit (ending).

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You must find a way to get into a scene (beginning), accomplish the work of the scene (middle), and exit gracefully (ending).

question: Map the clock inside each of your scenes and take complete awareness and control of it: decide how much time passes and what the reader experiences of it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Many of us would love to experience that loss of time more often, but in writing scenes we must have complete awareness and control of time.

question: Check that each of your scenes is anchored in a specific time and place, with events transpiring in real time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scenes are episodes that occur within a specific time and place, just like in films, and they give the reader a sense of events transpiring in real time.

question: Match your verbs to your scene's clock: slow verbs where time should crawl, a pile-up of action verbs where time should race.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Slow time requires slow verbs and fast time requires lots of action.

question: Keep the scenes and summaries of the younger self’s innocence so the older voice of wisdom has power—show the steps along the way to knowledge.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Without the scenes and summaries of his innocence, the voice of wisdom would have much less power.

question: Consider what second person does to your scene: it either makes the reader the primary character or suggests a narrator estranged from himself—either way it adds tension.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can use second-person point of view to accomplish two things: (1) It puts the reader in the position of being the primary character “you”, or (2) alternatively, it creates a sense that the narrator is detached from himself, alienated, estranged.

question: Place yourself inside the scene before writing: expand "see it" to smell, taste, or whatever other sensory details are needed, and describe the setting until it becomes real to you.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You could expand "See it" to include smell it, taste it, or whatever other sensory details are needed, but the essence of the mantra was that I needed to place myself inside the scene in order to write it authentically, and to do that I would have to describe the setting to the extent that it became real to me.

question: Develop the sensory details that pin your character to the moment—a hot puppy's skin, cool air, the tang of coffee—so the fall out of the moment lands dramatically.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Notice the level of detail in this scene, which contains no dialogue and no more action than a woman patting a puppy at a gas station. Dillard develops the sensory details that pin her to the moment—the puppy’s skin is hot, the air is cool, she tastes the tang of coffee on her tongue. Those grounding details make her fall from the experience of living in the moment all the more dramatic.

question: Ask what your setting does beyond establishing a believable background: could it carry symbolic meaning, reveal aspects of character, or establish mood and tone?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: One reason for working on setting is to create a credible experience for the reader—to make the scene feel real—but setting can and should do more than just establish a believable background to the action of the scene. Setting can have symbolic meaning, it can reveal aspects of character, establish mood and tone.

question: Compare your scene's setting against the mood you intend: would a change of season, time of day, or state of repair alter the emotional effect on the reader?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Same place, same situation—father and child returning to the father's childhood home, but a world of difference in mood. The setting is both the same and not the same. What was ominous has become cheerful and promising with just a change of season, time of day, and some fresh paint.

question: Read your setting for what it reveals about character: what would a bedroom tell about its owner—messy or orderly, whose pictures on the dresser?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: What can the details of the setting show about your character(s) in the scene? For example, what might a bedroom tell about your character? Is it messy or orderly? What pictures does she have on her dresser?

question: Elucidate the symbolic weight of any place or object in your scene: it must carry meaning beyond its factual identity, and that meaning must be a part of the narrative—on its own, a crumbling castle is just a crumbling castle.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To make setting function symbolically in a scene, the place or an aspect of it must carry a meaning beyond its factual identity and that meaning must be a part of the narrative. On its own it is just a crumbling castle.

question: Before a scene that follows another scene, add a setup summary that provides context or increases dramatic tension so the story flows smoothly instead of jumping choppily.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But when you need your story to flow smoothly, or if you want to increase the impact of a scene by preceding it with summary that provides context or increases dramatic tension, setups can be very useful.

question: Don’t let the show-don’t-tell rule silence your narrator—allow a strong reflective voice to ponder and interpret people and events.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: We’ve been so ingrained with the message “show, don’t tell” that we forget that some of the most powerful writers have strong reflective voices that ponder and interpret people and events.

question: Choose similes that advance your themes and set up what’s to come, not merely pleasant images: a lopped-off head sun works because it foreshadows violence.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: With this disturbing simile, Babel sets up the themes and violent actions to come; it is 1920 and the Russian Red Army has entered and is laying waste to villages in Poland. If he’d said, “the orange sun looked like a child’s bright balloon,” he would have missed the chance to advance his themes.

question: Locate the abstractions in your work and determine whether each deepens readers’ understanding or makes them turn away: demonstrate big ideas such as love, patriotism, or sacrifice in the particular, moving from the particular to the universal rather than the other way around.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Study your own work to see if you can locate abstractions. If you can, try to determine if the abstractions deepen readers’ understanding of the situation you’re describing or if the abstraction will make them turn away. Are you using big ideas such as love, patriotism, sacrifice as abstractions instead of demonstrating them in the particular, with the kind of detail that draws a reader in?

question: Cut exposition made of details and facts thrown in for their own sake — such as an entire genealogy for a minor character whose family history has no bearing on the central story.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Other unnecessary exposition occurs when details and facts are thrown in for their own sake without contributing to the overall work. If the writer gives us an entire genealogy of a character’s family when the character is minor or if the story of his great-great-great-grandparents has no bearing on the central story, that would be unnecessary exposition.

question: Identify the generalizations in your summaries — blanket statements about ethnicity, gender, age, or education, even generalized praise — and spend time transforming each one into a richly descriptive, individualized portrayal.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: See if you can identify any generalizations in your own summaries. Spend a little time with each one, asking yourself how you might transform the generalization into a richly descriptive portrayal.

question: Find events in your summaries that require evoking in scene — a moment of revelation or major change in the narrator’s or protagonist’s life — and rewrite them as scenes, not reported summaries.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Go back through your summaries and make sure that they don’t contain a reported version of an event that requires evoking in scene. If it is a moment of revelation or major change in the life of the narrator or protagonist, it probably should be a scene, not summary.

question: Where exposition only restates the shown action, replace it with detail that reveals a character oddity — a quirk the scene can't display, like a habit that exposes whether the character is clumsy or self-destructive.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: However, if the exposition stated that “Jack often bashed his thumb with hammers and doors and he’d even once stepped on his thumb while tying his shoe,” the summary would be useful because it would reveal an oddity about Jack’s character—either he is exceedingly clumsy or self-destructive.

question: Look over your reflections for grandiose or pedantic comments that set your narrator up as superhumanly wise or benevolent, check the pretentiousness-o-meter, and scale those observations and judgments back down to size.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Look over your reflections to make sure they don’t come across as grandiose or pedantic. If you find yourself making the kind of comments that set your narrator up as superhumanly wise or benevolent, check the pretentiousness-o-meter. Then scale those observations and judgments back down to size.

question: Cut exposition that merely repeats what your scene already shows or what your dialogue already speaks.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Any exposition that tells what is already being shown in a scene is definitely unnecessary. Exposition that duplicates what is spoken in dialogue is particularly onerous

question: Redline the reflective phrases that have a ring of familiarity — “He loved her with all his heart,” “There is no place like home” — and find a fresh way to get your point across. Push yourself: do you really agree with the familiar line?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Have any tired observations slipped into your work? Do you find lines such as “He loved her with all his heart” or “There is no place like home”? Give your work a read-through and redline phrases and sentences that have that ring of familiarity to them. Then find a fresh way to get your point across.

question: Question the necessity of each expository summary: is the information extraneous, or better shown through scenes? Try removing some of your exposition to see if anything has really been lost.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Question the necessity of your expository summaries. Are you offering information in your exposition that can be eliminated because it is extraneous (like that family genealogy) or better shown through scenes? Try removing some of your exposition to see if anything has really been lost.

question: Decide at each point whether scene or summary is called for, and slide between them gracefully.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Once you have learned the potential of both scene and summary, you must decide which is called for when, and how to slide between them gracefully.

question: Slow a scene’s pace by deliberately inserting background summary into the ongoing scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can slow the pace even further by inserting background summary into an ongoing scene, as described above.

question: Check that every shift from scene to summary feels smooth.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Does the shift from scene to summary feel smooth?

question: Watch out for characters who make speeches at length, especially with abstractions like courage, honor, or devotion—people rarely make speeches in conversation.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: people rarely make the kinds of speeches you hear in overly earnest or sentimental movies; people rarely make speeches at all in conversation. If your characters are going on at length and especially if they are using abstractions such as courage and honor or devotion, watch out!

question: Even a scene in which no one moves from a chair needs emotional movement—a revealing interaction or a shift in the reader’s perception—or it will feel static.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A scene might take place in a short time period in which no one moves from her chair. But if no emotional movement occurs in that scene of two people in their chairs, such as some kind of revealing interaction, or if the reader’s perception of those people doesn’t change over the course of the scene, the scene would feel pretty static.

question: Give a character a detail that breaks their stereotype—the distinguished-looking man video gambling on his laptop—to catch the reader's interest and make them want to know more.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If the distinguished-looking fellow is video gambling on his laptop, you might think he's in trouble. In either case, you've caught the reader's interest and made him want to know more about the character. The character has come alive for him through description—by showing, you have broken stereotypes and created reader interest.

question: Before using an ironic omniscient reflective narrator, study nineteenth-century omniscient narrators to absorb their diction, syntax, and general style so you can adapt them.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Often these omniscient reflective narrators take an ironic tone—a sort of winking at the reader to say, “We know this is old-fashioned; it’s a game we’re playing.” It’s a game you can play if you care to, but you’ll need to know your antecedents first, which means studying nineteenth-century omniscient reflective narrators to familiarize yourself with their diction, syntax, and general style in order to adapt them for your own purposes.

question: Render a conversation that recurs in repeated time as summarized dialogue—with phrases like “every time” and “then next time”—instead of staging it as a scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Although there’s dialogue, it is summarized. The phrases “every time my mother’s rung up” and “then next time” establish that this dialogue occurs in repeated time, not a scene:

question: Load your background summary with a second job — carrying a theme, setting an expectation, building suspense, or starting the story — after articulating your intentions for the piece.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can use background summary to provide necessary information and to carry themes, set up expectations, develop suspense, or even to get a story going once you fully articulate, to yourself, your intentions for the piece.

question: Make each background summary do heavy lifting — it halts the narrative, so cut any that don't earn their place with more than one job.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Background summary stops the flow of ongoing narrative just as flashbacks slow down scenes. Therefore you have to have good reasons for including it. It has to be doing heavy lifting for you; all the better if it does more than one thing.

question: When your scene can't naturally carry needed background — family history, past events — move that information into summary instead of stuffing it into dialogue or characters' in-scene thoughts.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: We may need to know characters’ personal or family history in order to understand them. Stuffing that kind of information into scenes by means of dialogue or characters thinking about past events in the midst of ongoing action can be clunky.

question: Keep summarized behavior specific even in general time — select individual characteristics that fit the character and tell who they are, never generic traits.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: However, summarized description and behavior should never be generic just because it occurs in general time. That means you’ll need to select individual characteristics that not only fit your character’s personality but tell who that character is.

question: Characterize obliquely in summary: let the objects and details a person keeps — the car they drive, the foods they prefer — reveal who they are.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Characters even can be made individual obliquely, via objects and details described in summary. (Think of what the car you drive, the foods you prefer, the way you dress at home reveal about you.)

question: Use summary to compress a stretch of time whenever the span of events matters more to the tale than any individual event within it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You compress time through summary when the span of events is more important to the tale than are the individual events.

question: Cut from your time-compressing summary every component included only because it happened; compression is selection, and selection gives what remains maximum impact.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You must have a good reason for including the components that you’ve chosen in your summary. Don’t just put them in because “they happened” or, in fiction, could have happened. Compression means selection, and selection allows the included components to have maximum impact.

question: Rewrite repeated actions with conditional verbs (would, could) and time adverbs (always, every, sometimes) instead of writing new scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The use of conditional verbs (would, could) and adverbs of time (always, every, sometimes) are the simplest and most commonly used approaches.

question: Cut the quickie establishing scene you wrote just to set context; deliver that background in summary instead.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: That kind of quickie establishing scene is better suited to the movies than to prose.

question: Elaborate a scene with surrounding summary that gives it context, so scene and summary enrich each other.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The summary gives context to the scene in the doctor’s office. The Margaret and Verbsky scene can proceed without the summary but the summary has enriched the scene, and vice versa.

question: Before writing a piece of fiction that relies on summary to the near exclusion of scene, consider that very few writers carry it off outside a book-length work; creative nonfiction, with its reliance on reflection, tolerates it better.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: there are very few writers who can carry off the piece that relies on summary to the near exclusion of scene, at least in fiction, and not in a book-length work. Creative nonfiction, with its greater reliance on reflection, may be less scene dependent.

question: Combine exterior and interior in summary: ask your characters what they wear, how they move, where they shop, then tell the answers to reveal how they think generally.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: What does this person wear? How does he move or speak? Where does she shop and what for? What does he do if he encounters a child or a dog? What does she watch on television, or does she even watch television at all? And so on—ask questions of your characters to find out who they are. Then use those answers to tell your readers who this person is and how she thinks generally.

question: Free write from the character's first-person point of view, even if the piece is third person. Memoirists can free write from their child-self; treat it as a throwaway exercise for entering their interior life.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: I often find it useful, with fiction, when I’m having difficulty getting inside a character (“normal” or not) to free write from the first-person point of view of that person, even if the novel or story is in third person.

question: Summarize the stretch between two scenes — the drive home, the errands, the routine — when none of the intervening events warrants a scene of its own.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can also compress time as your narrative moves forward through the use of summary.

question: Write summary in "general time" for events, information, and ideas not tied to a specific moment — nonscene memories, repeated actions, and reflections that stand alone or sit inside scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: However, summaries can be used when you wish to write about events, information, and ideas that do not take place in specific times. I call this “general time”—a kind of nonspecific “stepping out of time.”

question: To capture a character's irregular thinking in summarized musing, first identify what makes their thinking different, then inhabit the person and let the musings show how the mind works.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: First you have to identify what makes that person’s thinking different from “normal” people. Does the person think repeatedly about who has touched doorknobs and whether or not those doorknob touchers washed their hands after going to the bathroom? Or does she garble her thoughts and veer from sentimentality to anger as a drunk might? Is it an adult with a child’s mistaken trust of strangers? (Or is it, in fact, a child, with the attention to sensory detail that children possess?) After clarifying the difference in your own mind, you must perform a feat of imagination and inhabit that person.

question: Follow up a direct statement of a character's inner state (like "Benna misses everyone") with detailed, habitual evidence, or it reads as a bald assertion.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You’ll need to follow up that direct statement with more detailed information or the straightforward observation will come across as rather bald.

question: Describe a place through background summary as part of the piece's overall imaginative landscape — details that exist outside any specific scene and carry your characters' emotional situation.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can use background summary as a means of describing a place, and, if you so desire, the emotional situation of your character(s), by including details that exist not in a specific scene, a specific time, but as part of the overall imaginative landscape of your piece.

question: Cut summaries that run so long the emotional connection is lost, and give readers a breather where scenes pile up.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Does the summary go on so long that the emotional connection is lost? Do the scenes pile up, requiring a breather via summary?

question: Indicate repeated time with a list — an array of recurring items (the odd lunches, the things they carried) conveys recurrence without scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It also includes another technique you can use to indicate repeated time—listing. Here, in the context of the excerpt, the list of odd school lunches describes repeated disappointment.

question: Give minor characters backgrounds too — a few carefully selected words that work hard to round them out and enrich the piece.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But remember that not only your protagonist or your other main characters deserve backgrounds that will make them more real on the page. The key in using background summary for minor characters is very careful selection—you want a few words to work hard for you in creating as rounded a character as possible.

question: Test each summary: if it does not deepen themes, reveal character, or express your distinctive voice, it is a distancing shortcut—cut it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The trick with summary is determining when it’s a distancing shortcut or unnecessary explication, and when it’s a chance to deepen themes, reveal character, and express an author’s distinctive voice.

question: Open with background summary that reveals a character's history and sets the story in motion — even the catalytic event can come in summary rather than a scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Background summary placed at the beginning of a work can let us in on the history of a character and also set the story in motion,

question: When an emotion recurs — once is not enough — explore it in summary across a span of time instead of staging it in a single scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The answer is that Ralph always feels this way after talking to his mother. Once is not enough. Summary allows you to explore the emotion over a span of time.

question: Tell repeated actions in summary — the recurrence is the point — instead of staging a scene for each occurrence.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Summary is uniquely suited to describing actions and events that happen repeatedly. In repeated time summary, the emphasis is on the recurrent nature of the action rather than an event deserving an individual scene.

question: Show a repeated behavior through summarized, repetitious dialogue — the litany of a character's recurring complaints — rather than in individual scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you’re feeling more ambitious you can try indicating repetition through carefully selected phrases that indicate repetition or summarized, repetitious dialogue, as Wolff does.

question: Treat summary as the vehicle for information and scene as the vehicle for emotion: give the reader the larger picture in summary, then let the scene carry the visceral experience.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Our response to this extended scene is visceral. We experience Kingston’s emotions even as we have our own reactions to the events she dramatizes. The summarized parts that precede it evoke a more cerebral response, in which we are given information that will help us see the larger picture.

question: Choose setting details in your summary for what they reveal: pick ones that reflect your characters' emotional states and carry symbolic as well as factual weight.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Which details will give a clear picture of what matters or mattered to your characters—which details reflect their emotional states? What aspects of background setting might contain symbolic as well as factual weight?

question: Establish in background summary the impression of a character that a later scene will contradict and shatter; know that your piece turns on that contrast before setting the expectation.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you wish to set up expectations about a person’s character in order to shatter them, you first must know that your piece will turn on a contrast between the impression a person gives and an event that reveals another aspect of the character that contradicts that initial impression. The event, of course, should occur in a scene, but your background summary can establish the initial impression that you will later crush in the scene.

question: Get specific when you tell how someone behaves and feels in general — not in time and place, but in detail and emotion — or your summary has no impact.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The irony is that to tell how someone behaves and feels in general you have to get specific if you want your summary to have impact, just as O’Brien gets specific in the details that characterize the men in the platoon. You won’t be specific in time and place in the same way as in a scene, but specific in detail and emotion.

question: When your summary leaps across time, keep the reader located with locator tags ("a few months after," "the next week") or details that express time passing.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When you compress time through summary make sure your reader comes along with you by using tags or choosing details that express time passing.

question: Find the significant events and moments of change you have only summarized and render them in scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Have I summarized anything (significant events, moments of change, etc.) that needs to be in a scene?

question: Reach past the obvious verbs and adjectives when summarizing a character's habitual behavior; pick the ones that carry the most weight.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Consider the verbs and adjectives you might use in describing this guy. Reach past the obvious ones for the ones that carry the most weight.

question: Identify the material between your scenes—background exposition, description outside a scene, interior thoughts, repeated events, compressed action, and narrative commentary—and make sure it lives in summary, not scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Summaries are the material in between scenes—they may contain background exposition, description that doesn’t occur in a specific scene, interior thoughts, events that happen repeatedly or that are being recounted in a compressed fashion, and narrative commentary or reflection.

question: Interrogate a summarized interior statement with Why and How — what does the character actually feel, and how does that feeling show — then extend the summary with your answers.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ask yourself “Why?” Why does Ralph want to roll off his balcony after talking to his mother? What does he actually feel about her? Guilt? Frustration? Burdened? Angry? Helpless love (perhaps she has dementia)? All of the above? Now think of the “How.”

question: Rephrase your narrator's descriptions so the verb carries the attitude — "lurking" instead of "hanging around" — every word counts when revealing interior life.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your narrator thinks about a person who is always “lurking” around, the word lurking will convey an attitude that differs substantially than if the narrator mused that someone was always “hanging” around or “waiting” around or “appearing unexpectedly.” You have only words to work with; make them count when it comes to revealing interior life.

question: Raise an open-ended question in a scene—if readers are engaged enough to care about the answer, suspense will compel them to read on.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scenes can create suspense by raising an open-ended question: Will the girlfriend be tempted by her boyfriend’s best friend? Will the child pass the exam? Will Hamlet ever get over his indecision and take action to avenge his father’s murder? Will the new stepmother win over the angry and resentful stepchildren? Will Joe get his promotion when he’s called in to speak with his boss? Will the cop give you a ticket? If we’re so engaged with the characters and the situation that we care about the answer, the suspense will compel us to read on.

question: Create suspense by letting the reader know more than the character knows.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Suspense can be generated in a scene when the reader knows more than the character knows, as in all those teen slasher movies when the innocent party girl goes wandering down the dark hall at night and the audience thinks, Don’t open that door!

question: Vary your syntax and sentence length: unrelieved subject/verb/object constructions tire the reader, and extremely long convoluted sentences leave them gasping.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If all of your sentences are simple subject/verb/object constructions (He opened the door. He picked up the newspaper.) your reader will soon grow tired of the repetitive structure and probably believe that the character being described is some kind of somnambulist, moving in a waking dream.

question: Cut adverbs that follow dialogue tags: the action and the words themselves should show the manner of speaking (“Drop dead!” she said angrily is redundant).

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Be very sparing with adverbs following the tag. The action and words should show the manner in which the character is speaking. You don’t need “Drop dead!” she said angrily, since the dialogue shows her anger.

question: Use plain said or says for dialogue tags and cut pointed or whimsical verbs of speech (raged, harrumphed) that distract from the dialogue.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Avoid overly colorful verbs of speech. There’s nothing wrong with good old said or says. Pointed or whimsical verbs of speech tend can distract from the dialogue as in “Get out!” she raged, or “Can’t you kids quit bothering that cat?” the old lady harrumphed.

question: Make sure each dialogue tag is actually a verb of speech—“You’re cute,” she winked makes no sense.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Make sure your dialogue tag is actually a verb of speech. “You’re cute,” she winked makes no sense.

question: Match your reflective humor to your intent: for entertainment use narrative exaggeration; for literary aims let irony and absurdity shine without overwhelming the story or characters.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your aim is to entertain more than it is to illuminate, go ahead and make use of such humorous reflective techniques as narrative exaggeration. If your intention is primarily literary, look for the irony and the absurdity in your story and let it shine without allowing it overwhelm the story or the characters.

question: Rewrite the same scene in present, past, and future tense and compare: pick the version whose tense matches your intention, whether immediacy, consequences, or a jump from a larger framework.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can play around with alternatives to see which tense works best for a particular scene.

question: If you combine tenses in one scene, anchor each jump with time markers so the reader always stays located in time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can combine tenses as long as you're careful to keep the reader located in time. If you're going to combine tenses, be sure to use markers to avoid losing your reader.

question: Find every random tense switch in your scene—"He went downstairs and reaches for the orange juice"—and either give each switch a reason, an effect you are after, or make the tenses consistent.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You should not switch tenses unless there is a reason to do so, such as an effect you are after. Random jumping from one tense to another as in "He went downstairs and reaches for the orange juice" is both confusing and annoying to a reader.

question: Precede a scene with summary that offers relevant information and creates expectation for something important that is about to happen, so the reader is primed before the scene's events unfold.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Writers occasionally set up scenes by using summary that not only offers relevant information but creates expectation for something important that will happen in a scene.

question: Remember that not every scene needs conflict, but the piece as a whole must carry narrative tension—without opposition, characters' real natures are never tested or revealed.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Though not every scene has to contain conflict there must be narrative tension in the piece as a whole.

question: Test each summary insertion by making two versions of the scene—one without the insertions and one with them—then add the summary back bit by bit and cut any insertion that adds nothing essential.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To test the effectiveness of the summary you have inserted in a scene, make two versions of a scene, one without the insertions and one with them. Compare the two. Does the one without feel deficient or incomprehensible in any way? Now start adding in the summary, bit by bit, rereading the scene each time after an addition. Does each insertion add anything essential to the scene? If not, cut out that insertion. If so, leave it in.

question: Articulate what your story or essay is about on its deepest level—theme, distinct from plot—and make sure the scene emphasizes it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: (Theme is not plot; theme is what the story or essay is about on its deepest level.)

question: Check that your time markers haven't gotten so complex or lyrical that they misfire and the reader gets lost.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you decide to try a complicated method of locating your scene in time, make sure you haven't gotten so complex or lyrical that your marker misfires and your reader gets lost.

question: When you locate a scene in time, let the marker do double duty: instead of stating the facts directly, describe what the narrator sees—a watched sunrise that also establishes setting.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But whenever a description can do double duty (in this case locating us in time and place) without having to state the facts directly, the prose is particularly economical.

question: Locate each scene in a specific time with a simple time tag—"June first, 1963", "Last Thursday", "After she went into labor"—whenever the reader needs an anchor.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The easiest way (and a perfectly acceptable one) to locate the scene in a specific time is to use time tags such as June first, 1963 … One day … Last Thursday … Before we sat down for supper … After she went into labor … When the hike ended …

question: Move from scene to summary or scene to scene by carrying an associative link—a word, image, or sensory detail—across the shift.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A good method for moving from scene to summary or scene to scene is to use associative links: words, images, or other sensory details that can carry across different locations, time changes, or narrative modes.

question: Keep readers oriented by maintaining a straightforward chronology, and mark flashbacks clearly whenever you jump backward in time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Another simple way to keep your readers clear on what’s going on in your work is to generally maintain straightforward chronology (the story moving ever forward in time) with, if warranted, clearly indicated flashbacks.

question: Cut excessive cliff-hanger juxtapositions—too many and the device becomes obvious and tiresome.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You don’t want to set up too many cliff hangers or the device will become obvious and tiresome.

question: When you leave a scene for summary, add a connecting phrase that links logically and chronologically to what just happened in the scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A return to summary from the scene could be indicated by a connecting phrase such as “Melanie wondered about Bill’s tone for the rest of the day.” There’s a logical as well as a chronological link between the scene in the car and the summary of Melanie thinking about Bill.

question: Pivot from scene into summary through an image that carries psychological weight: let the character's eye land on an object in the scene that triggers her reflection.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Lahiri uses the wedding photo of Ruma and Adam on the bedside table as a device to shift from Ruma hanging up the phone (next to the picture, which catches her eye) to her ruminating on the state of her marriage. It’s a clever way of moving us via an image that carries psychological weight, right out of the scene and into summary.

question: Set one scene or summary against another so the juxtaposition itself forms the transition, for ironic or emotional effect.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You may want to set one scene or summary against another, creating a transition through juxtaposition of the two for ironic or emotional effect.

question: If your narrative is nonlinear, keep readers oriented by providing dates at the headings of each chapter.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Nonetheless, she helps us keep time straight by providing dates at the headings of each chapter.

question: Use a white space break on the page to mark a shift in time, place, or narrative mode between scenes and summaries—or even a chapter break.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Sometimes a transition can be as simple as a white space break on the page, indicating a shift in time and place or narrative mode (scene or summary), or even a chapter break.

question: When you come out of a summary into a scene, open with an indicator of time—like 'The following Saturday…'—so readers know exactly when and where they are.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: In this case, each time you come out of a summary you’d use some kind of indicator of time, such as “The following Saturday Melanie found herself on I-91, stuck in traffic, when her phone buzzed. It was Bill.”

question: If your scenes and summaries are short, cut back on space breaks and find other forms of transition, so your pages don't read like a list of vignettes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your scenes and summaries tend to be quite short you’ll end up with so many space breaks that your pages will look more like a list than narrative prose, and your novel or memoir may appear to be built on vignettes.

question: Render turning points in the action or a character's emotions as scenes, never as summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Turning points in the action or the character’s emotions must be rendered in scenes rather than summary.

question: Rewrite the setup so the character's habitual, ordinary behavior is established in summary, then break that habit in a scene where the character steps out of the summarized behavior—that break is your turning point.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When you establish a character’s behavior in summary by using general time—habitual, repeated, ordinary (as in Kingston’s portrayal of her silence and embarrassment)—and then you break that habit, confront the ordinary in a scene in which the character steps out of her summarized behavior (as in Kingston’s attack on the other girl), you have a turning point, a moment of change.

question: Before a scene, raise an unanswered question in the setup summary—relevant detail that creates an expectation in the reader—to build tension for what follows.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It has to be relevant and it has to create an expectation in the reader. Raising an unanswered question is one way of creating expectation.

question: Choose verbs for their emotional associations: he croaked versus he expired both mean dead, but each carries the narrator’s attitude and sets the tone.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Compare he croaked to he expired. In both examples, the subjects are equally dead. But each verb carries with it the narrator’s attitude toward the dead person as well as information about the manner in which each person died.

question: Write your summaries as narrative commentary in your own distinctive voice—voice often comes through best there.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A distinctive voice, that elusive quality we all desire as writers, often comes through best in summary.

question: Withhold a key fact from your reflective summary, dropping hints along the way, so the reveal lands with playful surprise in straightforward language.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Despite the title, and the fact that Orlean gives hints along the way, such as Biff eating hotel soap, we’re still surprised to learn that Biff is a boxer, a show dog. The effect is playful, though the language is straightforward.

question: Define the younger self’s situation in terms of geography, housing, family, school, and work.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Now define this younger person’s situation in terms of geography, housing, family, school, work, etc.

question: Go through a passage of your own prose and find every adverb whose meaning the verb already carries, and every adjective whose meaning the noun already carries. Rewrite so the verb or noun itself does the work.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: When the quality that the adverb indicates can be in the verb itself (they ran quickly raced) or the quality the adjective indicates can be put in the noun itself (a growling voice = à growl), the prose will be cleaner; more intense, more vivid.

question: Scan a page of your own writing and list the qualifiers you reach for again and again — your habitual 'very', 'just', 'kind of'. Cut every one that is not earning its place.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You might just look at your own writing to see if you have some very favorite qualifiers that you kind of use just a little too often.

question: Find every 'somehow' in your draft and replace it with the actual cause or mechanism. Nothing can happen somehow.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Nothing can happen somehow.

question: In your adjective-free, adverb-free passage, allow only the time adverbs that are genuinely necessary — then, next, later — and keep even those to a minimum.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Adverbs of time (then, next, later; etc.) may be necessary, but be sparing

question: Write your first adjective-free, adverb-free draft on new material, not on something you've already written. Save your old passages for later rounds of the exercise.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The first time you do the exercise, write something new.

question: Reread your adjective-free passage and ask: would adding an adjective or adverb here and there improve it, or is it satisfactory without? Keep it chaste unless a specific qualifier earns its way back in.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Would the piece be improved by the addition of an adjective or adverb here and there, or is it satisfactory without?

question: Look back at your adjective-free draft and notice the devices and usages the constraint forced you into — especially your choice of verbs and your use of simile and metaphor. Name what changed in your writing.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: notice the devices and usages you were forced into by the requirements of the exercise: It may have affected particularly your choice of verbs and your use of simile and metaphor

question: Repeat your descriptive scene in the voice of a character instead of the authorial voice — let a character in the story describe it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you find "Implication" an interesting exercise, you can repeat either or both parts: this time, instead of the authorial voice, use the voice of a character in the story to describe the scene.

question: Apply Chekhov's Razor to your draft: throw out the first three pages — starting a story, we all circle around, explain a lot of stuff, and set things up that don't need to be set up.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Anton Chekhov gave some advice about revising a story: first, he said, throw out the first three pages. But there are few first drafts to which Chekhov's Razor doesn't apply: Starting a story, we all tend to circle around, explain a lot of stuff, set things up that don't need to be set up. Then we find our way and get going, and the story begins very often just about on page 3.

question: Put two people into a crisis situation — the car out of gas, the spaceship about to crash — and let their talk carry the story.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you want a suggestion for the topic, put two people into some kind of crisis situation: the car just ran out of gas; the space ship is about to crash; the doctor has just realized that the old man she's treating for a heart attack is her father .

question: In your first draft crowd in everything boldly; then in revising decide what counts and what tells, and cut and recombine till what is left is what counts.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Tactically speaking, I'd say go ahead and crowd in the first draft, put everything in boldly. Then in revising decide what counts, what tells; and cut and recombine till what's left is what counts.

question: Audit what you crowd in and where you leap: everything crowded in to enrich the story sensually, intellectually, emotionally should be in focus, part of the story's center, and every leap should follow the trajectory of the whole.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Everything that is crowded in to enrich the story sensually, intellectually, emotionally, should be in focus, part of the central focus of the story. And every leap should be along the trajectory, following the shape and movement of the whole.

question: Check each paragraph of your story for slackness: keep the story full of what is happening in it, moving, not wandering into irrelevancies, and interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: By crowding I mean also keeping the story full, always full of what's happening in it; keeping it moving, not slack and wandering into irrelevancies; keeping it interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward.

question: Find the flabby phrases and cliches in your draft and replace them with the vivid phrase, the exact word: never use ten vague words where two will do.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: It's what we mean when we exhort ourselves to avoid flabby language and cliches, never to use ten vague words where two will do, always to seek the vivid phrase, the exact word.

question: Expect severe cutting to include some of your favorite, most beautiful and admirable sentences and passages, and cut them anyway; you are allowed to cry or moan while you do.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: This inevitably includes some of your favorite, most beautiful and admirable sentences and passages. You are allowed to cry or moan while you cut them.

question: In revision, cut any passage that sticks out or leaves the main trajectory; notice how often a cut that seemed sure to leave a terrible hole joins up without a seam.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And if any passage sticks out in some way, leaves the main trajectory, it could possibly come out. Often a cut that seemed sure to leave a terrible hole joins up without a seam.

question: Write a scene as pure dialogue — no stage directions, no description of the characters — so everything the reader knows comes through what the characters say.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write it like a play, with A and B as the characters' names No stage directions. No description of the characters. Nothing but what A says and what B says.

question: Practice psychological displacement: write a scene from inside a person of a different gender, age, or generation, even though it feels hard and scary.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: For some writers who have never practised this sort of psy chological displacement, it can be hard and scary just to change gender to write as a person of the opposite sex.

question: Cut every detail that doesn't tell: a mere inventory of articles bores the reader — make each detail build the mood you want.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A mere inventory of articles won't do it, and will bore the reader. Every detail must tell.

question: Find where your narrative pours out information as a lecture and break up the Expository Lump — grind the information into the story instead.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: and then he does , endlessly we have what science fiction writers call an Expository Lump.

question: Find the chunk of background information in your scene and compost it: break it up, spread it out, and slip it into conversation or action-narration as implication, passing reference, or hint.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: As you write the scene, "compost" the information, break it up, spread it out, slip it into conversation or action-narration or anywhere you can make implication, by passing reference, by hint, by any means you like.

question: Rewrite your scene so the process runs with at least two people present, either in the background of a conversation or as the locus of the action.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write a scene, involving at least two people; in which this process is going on, either in the background of a conversation, or as the locus of the action.

question: Choose something you know how to do that involves a complex series of specific actions — making bread, sailing a boat, repairing an engine — and build a scene around the process.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Think of something you know how to do that involves a complex series of specific actions: for example; making a loaf of bread or a piece of jewelry, building a barn, playing a game of blackjack or a game of polo, sailing a boat, repairing an engine, setting up a conference, setting a broken wrist, setting type

question: Make your scene understandable to a reader who has not read your background notes: include enough of the situation that it stands alone without them.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You don't have to write the whole story; just a scene or two that is based on this information and includes enough of it to be understandable to a reader who has not read the information.

question: Make the steps of the process clear to the reader, but keep it in the background — the process should not appear to be what the piece is about.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Whatever the process is, make the various steps clear to the reader, but don't let it appear to be what the piece is all about.

question: Learn to read your own work as a reader: you and you alone can judge it, and the judgment can be made rightly only by a writer who has learned to read her own work.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And ultimately you and you alone can judge your work.

question: Put a finished piece away and forbid yourself to look at it for at least a week, then reread it with a friendly critical eye, with revision in mind: to see its faults and virtues you need to look at it after a real interval.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: To see its faults and virtues we need to look at it after a real interval.

question: Read your finished piece aloud to yourself: speaking and hearing it will show up awkward bits and faults in the rhythm, and can help you make the dialogue natural and lively.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You might read the piece aloud to yourself, since speaking and hearing it may show up awkward bits and faults in the rhythm, and can help you make the dialogue natural and lively:

question: Reread your piece looking for what is awkward, unclear, excessive, and what breaks the pace or does not work — then cut or fix it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In general , look for whats awkward, unclear; excessive, what breaks the pace, what doesn't work.

question: Develop your craft deliberately: skill in writing frees you to write what you want to write, and it may also show you what you want to write.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Skill in writing frees you to write what you want to write. It may also show you what you want to write: Craft enables art.

question: Do not wait on luck: you can learn skill, you can earn it, and you can learn to deserve your gift.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But you can learn skill, you can earn it. You can learn to deserve your gift.

question: Write each scene as the account of an act or action, not a static scene: make something happen, so it ends up in a different place from where it started.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: it should end up in a different place from where it started. That's what narrative does. It goes. It moves.

question: Write to a short, set length and do not exceed it: the limit is itself excellent discipline.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: short, set length and not exceeding it is also an excellent disci pline in itself.

question: Write a paragraph seriously in the style of a writer you admire, not as parody or pastiche: imitation done seriously is a demanding and revealing exercise.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you write it not as parody or pastiche but seriously, it can be a demanding and revealing exercise.

question: Read masterful books attentively, with a consciousness of technique in mind: it is useful as well as enjoyable.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: An attentive reading of some of these books, with a consciousness of technique in mind , would be useful as well as enjoyable.

question: Practice invisible exposition: tell the reader things without appearing to tell — let the information ride inside the story.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: We're practicing invisible exposition.

question: Read your action scenes — a fist-fight, a battle, a sports event — for blow-by-blow accounts, which create confusion and boredom; leap instead, fast enough and far enough.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Action writers often crowd but fail to leap fast enough or far enough. We've all read descriptions of a fist-fight, or a battle, or a sports event, which by merely trying to give a blow-by-blow account create confusion and boredom.

question: In an action passage, include everything the reader needs to know and nothing more; make the sensory details intense, brief, and precise, and the language transparent.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Everything the reader needs to know is included, but nothing more. At each moment we know exactly where we are and what's happening. Every detail both enriches the picture and speeds the action. The language is transparent. The sensory details are intense, brief, precise.

question: Look at what you can leave out of your prose: what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in, so leave white space around the word, silence around the voice.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in. There has to be white space around the word, silence around the voice.

question: Leap over years at a time in your narrative, omitting great wads of the protagonist's life; omit the explanations and let the connections make themselves.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Woolf omits the explanations and lets the connections make themselves. The novel leaps over years at a time, omitting great wads of the protagonist's life.

question: Find any description where you tried to include everything and cut it down: overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you try to include everything in a description, you end up like poor Funes the Memorious in Borges's story, which, if you have not read, I recommend with all my heart. Overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.

question: Write from inside your story character: tell only what that single character perceives, feels, knows, remembers, and guesses.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: in "limited third" you' re writing from inside your story character: You can tell only what that single character perceives , feels , knows, remembers , guesses.

question: Cut anything in your limited-third-person scene that the viewpoint character cannot perceive — if Della wouldn't see her own violet eyes, don't describe them; if she is aware of them, show it through her action.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You can say, "Della looked up into Rodney' s adoring face; but you can't say, 'Della raised her incredibly beautiful violet eyes to Rodney's adoring face. Why not? Because although Della may be aware she's incredibly beautiful and has violet eyes, thats not what Della sees when she looks up. Thats what Rodney sees. And Della is the person whose mind you' re in.

question: Let a character talk through you: be quiet, listen, and write what they think and say as it rises from inside them.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Listen. Just be quiet, and listen.

question: Cut the expository freight from your memoir — the load of explaining and describing can stall it just as badly as it stalls science fiction.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: This expository freight can be as much a problem in memoir as it is in science fiction.

question: Let the people in your memoir speak in their own voices — if everyone says only what you wanted to hear, all we hear is an interminable monologue.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If all the people in the memoir say only what the author wanted to hear, all we hear is the author speaking an interminable monologue.

question: Revive a memory of someone you disliked or held in contempt and write the moment from that person's point of view, guessing how they felt, what they saw, and how they perceived you.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Revive a memory of a person you have disliked , or held in contempt, or felt to be very alien to you.

question: Test every line of dialogue against how people actually talk, and rework anything that sounds stagey.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Do people actually talk this way?

question: Write a sketch of an old woman at a present activity — washing dishes, gardening, whatever — as she thinks about an event from her youth, intercutting between "now" and "then" with at least two time-jumps.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You're going to write this sketch intercutting between the two times. "Now" is the kitchen, the garden, the desk, whatever, and "then is what happened when she was young. Your narration will move back and forth between "now" and "then. There should be at least two of these moves or time-jumps.

question: Write the sketch in a chosen person (first or third) and a chosen tense arrangement — all past, all present, "now" present with "then" past, or "now" past with "then" present — and label your choice.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Choose a PERSON: first person / third person (her namelshe). Choose a TENSE: all in past tense / all in present tense / "now" in present tense, "then' in past tense / "now" in past tense, "then" in present tense. Write the story. Label it Person (a) Tenses (c) or whichever you chose.

question: Now write the same story again in the other person and a different choice of tenses, and label it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Version Two: Now write the same story in the other person and a different choice of tenses. (Label it.)

question: When you write the second version, don't find-replace the pronouns and verb endings on a computer — write it over, and let the changed person and tense change the wording.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Don't strain to keep the wording of the two versions identical, and please don't just g0 through it on a computer changing the pronoun and the verb endings. Write it over:

question: Within one version, keep the person of the verb constant — only the tense may shift.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Within one version, the verb tense may shift, but the person of the verb can't.

question: Compare your two versions: which pronoun works best for the story, which tense suits the material, how awkward are the time-shifts, and what actually differs between the versions?

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: It may be useful to discuss the ease or awkwardness of the time-shifts; how well suited the tenses chosen are to the material; which pronoun works best for this story; which choice or combination of tenses works best for this story; whether there's much difference between the two ver sions and if there what is it

question: Read narrative prose with a particular consciousness of what persons and tenses of the verb are used, why the author used them, and how often the narrative tense changes.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: it can be useful to read narrative prose, for a while, with a particular consciousness of what persons and tenses of the verb are used

question: Find the passive constructions in your prose, name the doer, and make the doer the subject — convert them to active voice.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: It was proposed that the motion be tabled. Two passives. Ms. Brown proposed that the committee table the motion. Two actives.

question: Scan your prose for passives used because they are indirect and polite; rewrite them so someone takes responsibility — who thought it, who did it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: People often use the passive voice because its indirect, polite, unaggressive, and admirably suited to making thoughts seem as if nobody had personally thought them and deeds seem as if nobody had done them, so that nobody need take responsibility:

question: Check that the passive hasn't seeded itself into your style where it doesn't belong, and root it out.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Make sure it hasn't seeded itself where it doesn' t belong.

question: Before banning the passive voice, know what it is: the passive is not the verb to be.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But I find that many people who on about banning the passive voice don't even know what it is. have confused it with the verb to be

question: Use the past tense for easy movement in time: it gives access to times before and after the period of the narrative and implies continuity.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: By giving easy access to times before and after the period of the narrative, this tense includes a vast histori cal and narrative context. It implies continuity:

question: In past-tense narration, use the past perfect for a time before the narrative moment — "I hadn't seen," not "I didn't see."

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: since the simple past "I didn't see refers to a time previous to the present; but it occurs in a past-tense sentence, where a previous time would "I hadn't seen."

question: Look at your story apart from its plot — plot merely connects happenings in causal chains and is not superior to story, and not even necessary to it; some great stories have neither.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A story that has nothing but action and plot is a pretty poor affair; and some great stories have neither: To my mind, plot is merely one way of a story, connecting the happenings tightly, usually through causal chains. Plot is a marvelous device: But it's not superior to story; and not even necessary to it.

question: Tell the story of an accident twice: once in the detached author mode or in a journalistic, reportorial voice, then from the viewpoint of a character involved in the accident.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Or tell the story of an accident twice: once in the detached author mode, or in a journalistic, reportorial voice; then from the viewpoint of a character involved in the accident

question: Add a character who was there but not a participant, only an onlooker, and tell the same story in that character's voice.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If there wasn't a character in the original version who was there but was not a participant, only an onlooker; add such a character now.

question: If a story sticks and won't go right, try changing who tells it: the choice of point of view makes an immense difference to the tone, the effect, even the meaning of the story.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The choice of point(s) of view, the voice in which one narrates one's story; can make an immense difference to the tone, the effect, even the meaning of the story:

question: For every shift of viewpoint character in your story, be aware of it, have a reason for it, and stay in control of it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: must be aware of, have a reason and be in control of all shifts of viewpoint character.

question: Retell your scene in the detached-author voice: say only what a neutral observer (a fly on the wall) could infer from behavior and speech, and never enter a character's mind.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: There is no viewpoint character: The narrator is not one of the characters, and can say of the characters only what a neutral observer (an intelligent fly on the wall) might infer of them from behavior and speech. The author never enters a character' s mind.

question: Clarify that the "I" or third-person narrator of your fiction is not you, and decide how reliable that narrator is — unreliable narrators may deliberately or innocently misrepresent the facts.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In fiction, the "I" narrator (or the third-person narrator) is not the author: Most first- and third-person narrators in serious fiction used to be trustworthy, just like memoirists. But unreliable narrators are now fairly common in fiction, narrators who deliberately innocently misrepresent the facts.

question: Cut anything in your first-person scene that the viewpoint character could not know, feel, perceive, think, guess, or remember — the reader infers other people only from what "I" sees and says of them.
