source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: "I" tells the story and is centrally involved in it. what "I" knows, feels, perceives, thinks, guesses , remembers, etc , can be told.

question: Don't default to your genre's conventional POV: for romance, first person, observer-narrator, and involved author narration are equally suited to the genre.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Romances are conventionally told in limited third person, through the perceptions of the heroine, but first person, observernarrator, and involved author narration are equally suited to the genre

question: Hunt out inconsistent or frequent POV shifts in your story: unless handled with awareness and skill, they jerk the reader around, bouncing between incompatible identifications, confusing emotion, and garbling the story.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In fiction, inconsistent POV is a very frequent problem. Unless handled with awareness and skill, frequent POV shifts jerk the reader around, bouncing in and out of incompatible identi fications, confusing emotion, garbling the story:

question: When you expand a scene into the involved-author voice, give the story a context: find out what led up to it, and follow it further.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You may find you need to give it a context, find out what led up to it, or follow it further.

question: In an involved-author passage, let the narrative shift freely among characters' perceptions and into analysis or prediction only the author could make — a description of a room with nobody there to see it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The story is not told from within any single character. There may be numerous viewpoint characters, and the narrative voice may change at any time from one to another character within the perception, analysis, or prediction that only the author could make.

question: Understand your default to limited third person: it became the predominant modern fictional voice partly in reaction to the Victorian fondness for involved author narration and its abuses.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Limited third person is the predominant modern fictional voice partly in reaction to the Victorian fondness for involved author narration; and the many possible abuses of it.

question: Check your limited-third-person scene: nothing may be seen, known, or told except what the viewpoint character sees, knows, and tells — this limitation concentrates the voice and gives it authenticity.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: It has the same essential limitation: that nothing can be seen, known, or told except what the narrator sees, knows, and tells.

question: If you're a memoirist, practice limited third person by inventing a story with made-up characters — using it on factual narrative is trespassing, since you can't know what another real person thought and felt.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: To use limited third person in factual narrative is to trespass, pretending you know what another real person thought and felt.

question: In your memoir, flag any narration of another real person's private thoughts or motives as your guesswork, opinion, or interpretation — a memoirist can't be omniscient, even for a moment.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A memoirist doesn't have the right to do this without clearly indicating that Aunt Jane's thoughts and Uncle Fred's motives aren' t known facts, but the author's guess work, opinion; or interpretation. Memoirists can't be omniscient, even for a moment.

question: In your POV practice scenes, use little or no dialogue: while characters talk, their voices cover the POV, and you're not exploring that voice.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Please use little or no dialogue in these POV exercises While the characters talk, their voices cover the POV, and so you're not exploring that voice

question: When you move a passage from first to limited third person, don't just switch the pronoun and verb endings: treat it as a change of voice, because the reader's relationship to "I" is not the same as to "he" or "she".

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: First person is a different voice from limited third. The reader 's relationship to that voice is different because the author' s relationship to it is different.

question: If you use an observer-narrator, keep them a witness rather than the protagonist: the story is about events they witnessed, not about them.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The narrator is one of the characters , but not the principal character present, but not a major actor in the events. The difference from first-person narration is that the story is not about the narrator.

question: In your memoir or nonfiction narrative, remember that the "I" is the author: hold yourself to relating what happened, and don't change facts to make the story neater.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In autobiography and memoir; in nonfiction narrative of any kind, the "I" (whether the writer uses it or not) is the author. Reading nonfiction, we assume that the author is not inventing, but relating, and won't change facts to make the story neater at least, not blatantly.

question: Retell the same story from the point of view of one of the other people involved in it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Second: Retell the same story from the POV of one of the other people involved in it.

question: Treat any POV shift as a major change of voice: going from first to third person, or from involved author to observer-narrator, affects the whole tone and structure of your narrative.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Shifts within limited third person from one character' s mind to another's call for awareness and care. Its a major change of voice to go from first to third person, or from involved author to observer-narrator: The shift will affect the whole tone and structure of your narrative

question: For your involved-author practice, choose a story that concerns you, not one you use to preach.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: I do mean that the story should be about something that concerns you.

question: Present a character's unspoken thoughts directly, exactly as you would dialogue, but without quotation marks or italics — just make it clear the thought is going on inside someone's head.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Thoughts are handled exactly like dialogue, if you present them directly: But in presenting characters' thoughts you don' t have to use quotation marks, and I think italics or any typographical device overemphasizes the material.

question: Don't attempt quick, unsignalled POV shifting unless you command it with immense certainty and skill — it dissolves viewpoints into one another and is rare for a reason.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: This kind of quick, unsignalled shifting, discussed further below, is rare, and takes immense certainty and skill.

question: When you shift point of view, check that you know when and how you are doing it, so that the reader is carried effortlessly with you.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And you need to know when and how to do it, so that when you shift, you carry the reader effortlessly with you.

question: If you shift between first and third person in a short piece, ask whether you have a compelling reason for it — this shift is enormously difficult at that length.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Shifting between first and third person, as in the Another Additional Option to Exercise Six, is enormously difficult in a short piece.

question: Check your piece for a shift between a detached and an involved authorial voice — you cannot mix the two modes within one piece.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: You can't shift between detached and involved authorial voice within one piece.

question: Where your narration moves from one viewpoint character to another often, tighten control until the reader is never jerked from mind to mind or unsure whose mind they are in.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: but if it happens very often, unless the writing is superbly controlled (like Example Six) , read ers will tire of jerked from mind to mind, or will lose track of whose mind re supposed to be in.

question: Find any momentary slip into another character's viewpoint — even a single word of what they see or feel — and cut it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Remember when Della raised her violet eyes? That was a one-word POV shift. It doesn' t work.

question: Where you want distance, narrate in third person from the involved author's position, freely limiting perception to a single character for a while.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: the involved author can and usually does use thirdperson narration freely, and may limit perception for some while to a single person.

question: Rewrite your scene shifting among several viewpoint characters in limited third person, marking each change with a line break or the narrator's name.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Mark the changes with line breaks, with the narrator's name in head of that section

question: Rewrite your scene shifting point of view from character to character several times, deliberately, with no obvious signal to the reader that you are doing so.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: shifting POV from character to character several times without any obvious signal

question: Consciously and deliberately imitate a piece of prose you admire, as training toward finding your own narrative voice — the consciousness is what matters.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: I think conscious, deliberate imitation of a piece of prose one admires can be training, a means towards finding one's own voice as a narrative writer.

question: As the involved author, you may dip into another character's viewpoint for a single moment — do it with care, and never in limited third person.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: With care, the involved author can do this (Tolkien does it with the fox). But it cannot be done in limited third person.

question: Recognize that involved-author narration and limited third person overlap: with a subtle authorial voice, it can be hard to tell which mode a piece is written in.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: When the authorial voice is subtle, it can be hard to say for sure which mode a piece is written in.

question: Recognize that fear of plagiarizing and an individualistic valuation of originality can stop you from using deliberate imitation as a learning tool.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A rational fear of plagiarizing, and an individualistic valuation of originality have stopped many prose writers from deliberate imitation as a learning tool.

question: Know that in the present tense narration is linear, leading moment to next moment and excluding global temporal reference — it implies discontinuity.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In the present tense, narration is linear, leading to the next moment, excluding global temporal reference:. ... The present tense implies discontinuity:

question: If you write in the present tense, keep out simple and compound past forms and the future — they become awkward and highly artificial.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: use of the simple or compound past tenses becomes awkward and use of the future highly artificial.

question: Don't mistake a narrow focus for immediacy — the present tense's narrow focus merely leaves out more.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A narrow focus isn' t more immediate: it merely leaves out more.

question: Be aware that the present tense flattens the affect of your voice and produces a curious sameness in narrative.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: From this flatness derives the curious sameness of present-tense narrative. It all sounds rather alike:

question: In present-tense narrative, write "then," not "now" — this is a story, not actuality.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: We write, "She slaps the Velcro fasteners on her Adidas, then gets up and stretches. ... We use then because this isn't the present, isn't actual.

question: Name the punctuation marks you avoid out of fear or uncertainty. Practice using them until they feel like tools in your kit, not rules to trip you.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you aren't interested in punctuation, or are afraid of it, you' re missing out on a whole kit of the most essential , beauti ful, elegant tools a writer has to work with

question: Go through a draft and mark every place you used language carelessly or stupidly. Rewrite those sentences, because language misused breeds lies and half-truths even with the best intentions.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: We need to remember that it works the other way round too. Even with the best intentions , language misused , language used stupidly; care lessly, brutally, language used wrongly; breeds lies, half-truths , confusion.

question: Treat using language well as your first duty as a writer. For each sentence you write, ask whether your use of language is honest.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In that sense you can say that grammar is morality. And it is in that sense that Isay a writer' s first duty is to use language well.

question: Before you 'correct' a sentence, ask whether the rule serves clarity or just marks you as a member of a grammatical in-group. Do not let correctness become a shibboleth that divides writers.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Correct grammar; correct usage, are used as tests or shibboleths to form an ingroup of those who speak and write English 'correctly' and an out-group of those who don' t. And guess which group has the power?

question: Scan your written prose for incorrect usage that is not part of a conscious, consistent dialect voice. Rewrite it, because left alone it can invalidate the whole piece.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: "incorrect usage, in written prose, unless part of a conscious, consistent dialect voice, is disastrous.

question: Find the half-finished sentences and misused words in your writing that would pass aloud but fail on the page. Rewrite them so the words alone are clear, without voice or intonation to help.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Our standards for writing are higher and more formal than for speaking.

question: Find a place where you broke a grammar or punctuation rule. Rephrase the sentence so the break reads as a knowing choice, not an error — you may only break the rules you know.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Only if you know the rule can you break it.

question: Scan your prose for ungrammatical, overcorrected, or colloquial usages that stick out on the page. Cut them — they make the sentence sound all wrong even when they are not morally wrong.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: For all of us, this involves avoiding ungrammatical, overcor rected, or colloquial' usages that stick out painfully in written prose.

question: List the punctuation problems you have with your own writing: what you feel uncertain about, and which rules you are impatient with — those are the places where your prose will slip.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: What problems do you have with punctuation? What do you feel uncertain about? What rules are you impatient with?

question: Look up every punctuation usage that worries you. Study model examples from writers you trust and practice imitating them until the usage feels easy.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In the term, it's worth looking up the things that worry you.

question: Take a few paragraphs of prose you admire and study the punctuation in them: why did the author break that sentence there, where did she want a pause, how much of the rhythm is carried by the punctuation?

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: did she break that sentence that way, did she want a pause there, how much of the rhythm of the prose is actually established by the punctuation, how's it done?

question: Rewrite a passage of your own narrative with all punctuation removed — no paragraphs, no breaks — so it must make itself clear without punctuation. Then punctuate it again, rewriting wherever the punctuation was doing the work, and ask which version is stronger.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The nonpunctuated passage had to find a way to make itself clear without punctuation. To punctuate it may involve rewriting it.

question: Read through a draft for sentences where a missing or misplaced comma changes the meaning. Make sure each comma commits the sentence to what you actually mean.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Eats shoots and leaves.

question: Find the movement in your story's quietest moments: a letter sent that doesn't arrive, a thought unspoken, the passage of a summer — that can be action enough.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: a story must move, something must happen; but the action can be nothing more than a letter sent that doesn't ar rive, a thought unspoken; the passage of a summer

question: Read your writing out loud — not in a whisper — and hear how natural or stagey it sounds, where the emphasis goes wrong.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you're working yourself , read it out loud.

question: Repeat a small, quiet description word for word later in the story, so the changed context gives it a different, deeper resonance.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: the last two sentences of this little description are repeated word for word, with an utterly different, heartbreaking resonance. (Oh, the power of repetition!)

question: Find a spot where you swapped a repeated word for a farfetched thesaurus substitute; keep the honest repetition instead.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: GAIN [ AM INCLINED TO FAULT JOURNALISTS AND SCHOOLTEACHERS, however well meaning, for declaring it a sin to say the same word twice, driving people to the thesaurus in desperate searches for farfetched substitutes.

question: Scan your draft for a word repeated without carrying emphasis; fix it with a synonym or a different phrasing.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Repetition can indeed be awkward when a word is emphasized for no reason:

question: Find a paragraph where you avoided repeating a word out of rule, and let the repetition back in.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But to make a rule never use the same word twice in one paragraph; or to state flatly that repetition is to be avoided, is to throw away one of the most valuable tools of narrative prose.

question: Inventory the repetition in your story beyond single words: repeated phrases, images, the word 'said', near-repetition of events, echoes, reflections, variations.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Repetition of words, of phrases , of images; repetition of said; near-repetition of events; echoes , reflections , variations:

question: Find where your prose repeats a beat as obviously as poetry's rhyme and chime, and revise so the sameness is subtler.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Prose can't rhyme and chime and repeat a beat as poetry can, or if it does it had better be subtler about it than the first half of this sentence.

question: Hunt out the repetition that gives your prose its rhythm — it works hidden and obscure, not obvious.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The rhythms of prose and repetition is the cenmeans of achieving rhythm are usually hidden or obscure, not obvious.

question: Rewrite a passage with open, fearless repetition and read it aloud; let the repeated words carry their due majesty and power.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: All such narration is completely fearless about repetition, it openly and often, both to the story and to give the words their due majesty and power.

question: Write a passage meant to be read aloud that uses repetition as incantation — as a structural device and for laughter.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Stories written to read aloud to children use a lot of repetition. Kipling's Just So Stories (see Example Two) are a splendid example of repetition used as incantation, as a structural device, and to make you and the child laugh.

question: Give a character a catchphrase and repeat it, verbatim or nearly so, throughout the story; the reader will wait for it and it will grow funny.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Repetition is often funny The first time David Copperfield hears Mr: Micawber say, "Something is certain to turn up; 7 it doesn' t mean much to David or to us, but the time we' ve heard or nearly the same words throughout the book, it is very funny: The reader waits for it, as for the inevitable and delight ful repetition of a musical in Haydn.

question: Notice how each return of a repeated phrase gathers weight; let the darkness underneath the funniness grow darker with every repetition.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But also, every time gathers weight. The dark ness underneath the funniness grows always a little darker:

question: Map the happenings in your story and find the events that echo one another.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Structural repetition is the similarity of the events in a story; happenings that echo one another.

question: Reread your opening chapter and list the images and themes it plants that the rest of the book repeats, with variations.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The first chapter contains a deal of "foreshadowing, the introduction of images and themes that will be repeated throughout the book.

question: Rewrite a paragraph of narrative (about 150 words) so a noticeable noun, verb, or adjective appears at least three times — not an invisible word like 'said' or 'was'.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write a paragraph of narrative (150 words) that includes at least three repetitions of a noun, verb, or adjective (a noticeable word, not an invisible one like 'said, "did") "was,

question: Elaborate a paragraph to a page of narrative (200-400 words) in which one syntactical construction, or one exact rhythm, repeats several times.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write a paragraph to a page of narrative (200-400 words) in which you deliberately repeat the syntactical construction, or the exact rhythm; of a phrase or sentence (or more than one) several times.

question: Connect two sentences that share an exact rhythm with a one-word swing like 'But'.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The "But"' is a swing-word connecting two sentences that are exactly alike in their rhythm.

question: If you can't hear that two sentences share a rhythm, say them aloud — chant them — until you hear the sameness.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you don'thear the sameness , say them aloud, chant them, and you will.

question: Treat exact syntactic repetition as an exercise in awareness, not as a technique to leave in finished story prose.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Deliberate, exact repetition of this kind is not a technique to use in story-writing; its an exercise in awareness.

question: Carry exact repetition only as far as you can before the prose goes monotonous; check and revise against the monotony as you write.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you carry it on very of course, the prose gets monotonous.

question: Write a short narrative (350-1000 words) in which something said or done is later echoed or repeated — in a different context, by different people, or on a different scale.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write a short narrative (350-1000 words) in which something is said or done, and then something is said or done that echoes or repeats it, perhaps in a different context, or by different people, or on a different scale

question: When critiquing, concentrate on the effectiveness of the repetitions and whether they are obvious or subtle.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In critiquing, you might concentrate on the effectiveness of the repetitions and their obviousness or subtlety:

question: In memoir and nonfiction, beware forcing unlike events into a repetitive pattern — it distorts the events of a life.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Imnot sure how free the nonfiction writer is to use structural repetition. To force unlike events into a repetitive pattern cer the events of a life surely is one of the memoirist' s

question: Collect examples of structural repetition from fiction and nonfiction you admire; noticing how repetition and echoing build structure will sharpen your appreciation.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Look for examples of structural repetition in fiction and nonfiction (and if you have a group, share and recommend them)

question: Treat revision consciously as a time to consider what could go out if it had to: cut repetitions, unnecessary explanations, and everything that merely pads.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Unless you are unusually sparing with your words, or wise and experienced enough to cut as you write, revision will almost always involve some cutting of repetitions, unnecessary explanations, and so on. Consider revision consciously as a time to consider what could go out if it had to.

question: In your description, reach for senses other than sight — sound above all, and a particular scent or stink that sets the feeling-tone.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In descriptive writing, give a thought from time to time to the senses other than sight . Sound, above all, is evocative: We havea limited vocabulary for smell , but mention of a certain scent or stink can set a feeling-tone:

question: Rewrite your scene so each sentence leads to the next until the scene ends.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And so, until the scene ends, each sentence should lead to the next sentence.

question: Treat sentence length as a rhythm instrument: as you revise, consider how the length of each sentence beats the pace of your prose.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Sentence length has a lot to do with the rhythm of prose.

question: Vary your sentence lengths: a page of all-short sentences sounds stupid, a page of all-long ones sounds stuffy.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: As Strunk and White say, variety in sentence length is what's needed. All short will sound stupid.

question: Match each sentence's length to what it says and does: let a complicated perception or feeling work itself out in a long sentence, and keep a simple action in a short one.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: This kind of subject may well require a complicated sentence that can work itself out at some length.

question: Write a long sentence so its length gives weight to the last clause; read it aloud to hear where the weight falls.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you read it aloud you'Il hear how the length of the sentence gives weight to the last clause of it.

question: Find two sentences you would normally separate with a period and rephrase them as one sentence joined by a semicolon, so the connection between them stays visible and the flow continues.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: so that most of these sentences would have been equally 'correct" if Austen had used periods instead of semicolons.

question: Build sentences more deliberately than you speak them: because you can revise, you are not bound to speech-like short prose.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Itsa myth that short-sentence prose is more like the way we speak. A writer can build a sentence in a more deliberate way than a speaker can, because a writer can revise.

question: Write a half-page to a page of narrative, up to 350 words, that is all one sentence.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Part Two: Write a half-page to a page of narrative, up to 350 words, which is all one sentence.

question: Write a paragraph of narrative, 100 to 150 words, in sentences of seven or fewer words; no fragments — every sentence must have a subject and a verb.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Part One: Write a paragraph of narrative, 100-150 words, in sentences of seven or fewer words. No sentence fragments!* Each must have a subject and a verb

question: Use a very long sentence when powerful, gathering emotion is building, or when you want to sweep a lot of characters in together.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: For Part Two: A very long sentence is suited to powerful, gathering emotion, and to sweeping a lot of characters in together.

question: Elucidate any long sentence whose syntax could lose the reader; make the syntax clear and assured so no one has to go back and start over.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Is the syntax of the sentence clear and assured, so that the reader doesn't get lost and have to go back and start over?

question: Cut the mechanical rule that sentences and paragraphs must be kept short: it comes from journalism, not from good prose, so let the story, not the rule, decide where your sentences and paragraphs break.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Rules about keeping sentences and paragraphs short are mechanical spin-offs from journalism and a highly artificial school of action writing.

question: Tell the same story twice, once in short sentences and once in long ones, and see what the sentence length does to the story.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If you told two different stories in the two different sentence lengths, you might try telling the same story in both, and see what happens to the story.

question: Don't read "show, don't tell" as listing actions and objects without interpreting — keep your judgment and emotion in the text.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: List actions and objects, but don' t interpret, lest you be seen as judgmental; don' t show emotion, lest you be seen as unsophisticated

question: Hear your prose as sound before meaning: the basic elements of language are physical — the noise words make and the rhythm of their relation.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The basic elements of language are physical: the noise words make and the rhythm of their relation

question: Cultivate an awareness of what your own writing sounds like — it is an essential skill for a writer, and one you can relearn.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: an awareness of what your own writing sounds like is an essential skill for a writer.

question: Train your mind's ear: readers hear the sound of your prose even when they read in silence, so listen to your own writing the way they do.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A reader has a mind's ear. Though we read most of our narratives in silence, a keen inner ear does hear them

question: Listen for the faults in the sound of your prose — dull, droning, jerky, feeble — and cut them. Keep what is lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, and beautiful.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Dull , droning, jerky, feeble: these are all faults in the sound of prose, though we may not know we hear them as we read. Lively, well-paced, flowing; strong, beautiful: these are all qualities of the sound of prose, and we rejoice in them as we read

question: Make each narrative sentence lead to the next — that is its chief duty, keeping the story going.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Now the chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence

question: Read your writing aloud, and loudly — that is how you hear what your prose sounds like.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: (Read them aloud! Read them aloud loudly!)

question: You have to hear your writing to feel its rhythm — pace and movement depend above all on rhythm.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But pace and movement depend above all on rhythm, and you have to hear your writing to feel its rhythm.

question: Gorgeousness is not one style: there are lots of ways to be gorgeous, so find the way that fits your own prose instead of imitating one model.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: There are lots of ways to be gorgeous.

question: Write with exuberant vocabulary and musical, dramatic phrasing — give your readers a lifelong sense of the pure beauty of language.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The Just So Stories are a masterpiece of exuberant vocabulary, musical and dramatic phrasing' and humor.

question: Choose your characters' names for their sound: names are under the fiction writer's control.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Names are very interesting sounds; and names are often under the fiction writer's control

question: Write a paragraph to a page (150-300 words) of narrative that's meant to be read aloud, using onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect — any sound effect you like. Don't use rhyme or regular meter: this is a prose exercise.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write a paragraph to a page (150-300 words) of narrative that's meant to be read aloud. Use onomatopoeia, alliteration; repetition, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect any kind of soundeffect you like

question: Rewrite your scene so that what happens happens in the sounds of the words and the rhythms of the sentences — let the events take place in the sound itself.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Make what happens happen in the sounds of the words, the rhythms of the sentences.

question: Reframe your read-aloud piece as one written for children, if that's the only way you can give yourself permission to cut loose and play with sound.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Write it for children, if that's the only way you can give yourself permission to do it.

question: Take the view out the window, the mess on the desk, or something weird somebody said, and make a gorgeous sentence or two or three out of it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Look at the view out the window or the mess on the desk, or remember something that happened yesterday or something weird that somebody said, and make a gorgeous sentence or two or three out of it.

question: Take your sound piece and play some more with it — improve it here and there, make the sound of it still stronger and livelier.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: play some more with it, make the sound of it still stronger and livelier.

question: Ask yourself whether concentrating on the sound of your writing released or enabled anything unusual or surprising — a voice you haven't often used.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Did concentrating on the sound of the writing release or enable anything unusual or surprising, a voice you haven't often used?

question: Describe the stage without the actors on it: say nothing directly about the absent person or untold event that is the real subject — let the place suggest it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: This is the stage without the actors on it; this is the camera panning before the action starts. And this kind of suggestion is something words can do better than any other medium, even film.

question: Start a story from just a character, a conversation, a situation, or a place — no elaborate plot plan needed — and find the story there.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: All you need may be a character or two,or a conversation, or a situation, or a place, and you'll find the story there.

question: Check whether you have conflated story with conflict: conflict is one kind of behavior; a complex narrative needs the others too — relating, finding, bearing, losing, discovering, parting, changing.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: No narrative of any complexity can be built on or reduced to a single element. Conflict is one kind of behavior. There are others, equally important in any human life, such as relating, finding, bearing, losing, discovering, parting, changing.

question: Test your story against the definition: a narrative of events, external or psychological, which moves through time or implies the passage of time, and which involves change. Where is the change?

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: I define story as a narrative of events (external or psychological) which moves through time or implies the passage of time, and which involves change.

question: State your story's focus — what it is about, who it is about: the explicit or implicit center to which all the events, characters, sayings, and doings refer.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: We don't have to have the rigid structure of a plot to tell a story; but we do need a focus. What is it about? Who is it about? This focus, explicit or implicit, is the center to which all the events, characters, sayings, doings of the story originally or finally refer.

question: Check whether your story can be retold as a plot without fatal loss: if the story is not in the plot but in the telling, make sure the telling, not the plot summary, carries it.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But most serious modern fictions can't be reduced to a plot, or retold without fatal loss except in their own words. The story is not in the plot but in the telling; it is the telling that moves.

question: If you are a beginning writer, consider building your narrative on the armature of a strong, shapely plot: a pleasure in itself, reusable generation after generation.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A strong, shapely plot is a pleasure in itself. It can be reused generation after generation: It provides an armature for narrative that beginning writers may find invaluable.

question: Trace your story's trajectory: the movement — straight ahead, roundabout, recurrent, or eccentric — which never ceases, from which no passage departs entirely, and to which all passages contribute.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: And a story equally needs what Jill Paton Walsh calls a trajectory: not necessarily an outline or synopsis to follow, but a movement to follow: the shape of a movement, whether it be straight ahead or roundabout or recurrent or eccentric, a movement which never ceases, from which no passage departs entirely, and to which all passages contribute in some way.

question: Where your scene is nothing but voices, create the story-world and its people around the dialogue — with only disembodied voices, too much is missing.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: In fiction, a tremendous amount of story and character may be given through the dialogue, but the story-world and its people have to be created by the storyteller: If there's nothing in it but disembodied voices, too much is missing:

question: Choose a viewpoint character you can actually write inside: someone profoundly different from you socially, culturally, or by language or nation may not be accessible to you as a character.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: A person who is profoundly different from you socially, turally, by language, by nation, may in fact not be accessible to you as a character.

question: Write from inside a viewpoint character you dislike, suspending judgment — walk a mile in their moccasins and see the world through their eyes instead of exposing how awful they are.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: That is a legitimate and canny writing tactic. But it defeats the purpose of the exercise, which is to suspend your judgment on this person. What the exercise asks is to walk a mile in their moccasins, seeing the world through their eyes.

question: Get yourself, your ego, your opinions, your mental junk out of the way: find the focus of the story and follow the movement of the story, and let the story tell itself.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If I can keep myself, my ego, my opinions, my mental junk, out of the way and find the focus of the story and follow the movement of the story, the story tells itself.

question: Remember that in narrative, the past tense is not past and the present tense is not present — both are entirely fictive.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: past tense is not past and the present tense is not present. Both are entirely fictive.

question: Write abstract discourse and generalities in the present tense — generalities aren't time-bound.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Abstract discourse such as this essay is always in the present tense. Generalities aren' t time-bound.

question: Don't write present-tense generalities about people or practices that belong to the past — describe what is past as past.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: anthropologists used to write, "The Ussu worship forest spirits; even when the last three Ussu were Mormon converts working for the lumber mill.

question: Practice the past tenses you're hesitant about until they come freely — regaining free use of them increases your range of options as a storyteller.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: To regain free use of them is to increase your range of options as a storyteller. There are times the present tense is the right one, and there are times the past tense is the right one. Let yourself be able to make the choice.

question: Signal every switch of narrative tense with a line break, a dingbat, or a new chapter — otherwise your reader gets mixed up about what happened before what.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: if you switch the tense of your narrative frequently and without some kind of signal (a line break, a dingbat,; anew chapter) your reader will all mixed up as to what pened before what and what's happening after which and when we are, Or were, at the moment.

question: Before changing tenses mid-story, ask yourself whether you have a reason for the change — a tense switch is a big deal, like changing viewpoint characters.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: So its worthwhile to think, before changing tenses in mid story, whether you have any reason for so.

question: Take a piece of narrative prose you have written, 400-1000 words, and cut it by half: count the words, reduce them to half that many, and keep the narrative clear and the sensory impact vivid.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Take one of the longer narrative exercises you wrote, perhaps Exercise Seven, Part Four, and cut it by half. It means counting the words and reducing them to half that many while keeping the narrative clear and the sensory impact vivid, not replacing specifics by generalities, and never using the word somehow.

question: If your piece has dialogue, cut every long speech and conversation in half just as implacably as you cut the narration.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: If there's dialogue in your piece, cut any long speech or conversation in half just as implacably.

question: After severe cutting, weigh your words and name which proved to be styrofoam and which gold: severe cutting intensifies your style, forcing you both to crowd and to leap.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Forced to weigh your words, you find out which are the styrofoam and which are the gold. Severe cutting intensifies your style, forcing you both to crowd and to leap.

question: Rewrite your There-is and There-are constructions with exact, colorful verbs — "Three great oaks stand on the road to Doomthorpe" is stronger than "There are three great oaks on the road to Doomthorpe."

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: verbs are more exact and colorful than the verb to ... for instance, the sentence above might be stronger as: "Three great oaks stand on the road to Doomthorpe:"

question: Don't ban the There-is construction outright — it is not inherently wrong and has its uses in the right place.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: But there is nothing inherently wrong with There-is, and there are reasons for it

question: Give a glimpse of an event's mood and nature by describing the place where it happened or is about to happen — never the event itself.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Give us a glimpse of the mood and nature of some event or deed by describing the place room, rooftop, street, park, landscape, whatever where it happened or is about to happen.

question: Differentiate each character's voice until a reader could tell the speakers apart without name tags.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: Could we tell the two voices apart without the A and B signals, and if not, how might be more differenti ated?

question: Create and explain the world of your story inside the story itself — the reader has no way to know it unless the narrative tells them.

source.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
source.quote: The world of the story must be created and ex plained in the story:

question: Compress your poem to austerity — strip every word that does not earn its place, since poetry usually involves austere compression.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Poetry usually involves austere compression.

question: Fix the major problems in your manuscript before starting a page-by-page, front-to-back revision, so you don’t grow cold on the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: To avoid growing cold, I advocate fixing major things before starting on a page-by-page, front-to-back revision.

question: Check whether your article builds toward a climax instead of making one point after another on a plateau.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you are writing an article, does it make one point after another on a plateau, or does it build toward a climax?

question: Search your draft for a buried anecdote that could be made stronger than your present opening, and consider promoting it to the top.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Sometimes the germ of such an anecdote is buried elsewhere in the draft. If so, examine it to see if it has the potential of being made stronger than your present opening.

question: Hunt for the moments in your draft that could produce ten seconds of boredom — an audience has almost no tolerance for a mishap — and cut them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: First, the necessity of sitting through bad plays, to witness coughing and squirming in the audience, to have ears up like a rabbit to catch what didn’t work, to observe how little tolerance an audience has for a mishap, ten seconds of boredom breaking an hour-long spell.

question: Treat everything in your writing as calculated for effect — every word and its order chosen deliberately, the way Lincoln calculated almost everything for effect.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The historian Shelby Foote reminds us, “Lincoln was highly intelligent. Almost everything he did was calculated for effect.” That statement is one no writer should ever forget.

question: Edit each sentence against the two objectives of all prose — clarity and precision — and rework anything that fails either.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What I learned from my destroyed work were the two simple objectives of all prose writing, to be clear and to be precise.

question: Write at the same time every day and re-revise without balking — set aside the excuses, since difficulties do not excuse the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Others find excuses for not writing at the same time every day, balk at re-revising incessantly, or excuse themselves because their lives are beset by difficulties.

question: Take a story you admire and dissect it over and over — read it repeatedly until it surrenders the secrets of how it works.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It was from this practice that I learned the value of dissecting a piece of writing repeatedly until it surrendered its secrets.

question: Rewrite the dry passages of your draft so they enable the reader to see as they read, move them, and stimulate the intellect with insight — otherwise the writing fails its purpose.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What we mean by “dry” is that it does not enable us to see as we read, it does not move us, and, most important, it does not stimulate our intellect with insight, its ostensible purpose.

question: Rephrase the passage so it evokes an emotion in the reader rather than merely communicating how you feel — the emotional effect is better suited to your purpose.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Even when we write love letters, we are trying to communicate how we feel and not necessarily trying to evoke an emotion in the recipient, though that might be better suited to our purpose.

question: Practice consciously providing an extraordinary experience for the reader — craft so the reader is oblivious to the fact that they are seeing words on paper.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What it requires is the conscious practice of providing an extraordinary experience for the reader, who should be oblivious to the fact that he is seeing words on paper.

question: Remove raw information from your fiction: when information obtrudes, the experience of the story pauses and the author seems to be filling in — cut anything that distracts from the experience even momentarily.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In fiction, when information obtrudes the experience of the story pauses. Raw information comes across as an interruption, the author filling in. The fiction writer must avoid anything that distracts from the experience even momentarily.

question: Elaborate your report by setting what you saw in a framework — what has happened elsewhere or in the past — so the scrim lifts, sight becomes insight, and reporting becomes art.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The best of nonfiction, however, sets what it sees in a framework, what has happened elsewhere or in the past. As the recorded events march before us, a scrim lifts to convey another dimension, the highlighting focuses our attention, sight becomes insight, reporting becomes art.

question: Find the flat, cliché-ridden phrases in your draft and rewrite them with fresh simile and metaphor — the electricity of fresh imagery empowers the reader’s feelings and compels attention.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When a writer or speaker understands the electricity of fresh simile and metaphor, his choice of words empowers our feelings, his language compels our attention, acceptance, and action.

question: Check the intention behind your draft: if it is self-expression, a message, or being liked by readers, reset it so your purpose is providing the reader an experience superior to what they encounter in everyday life.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Those are all occasional outcomes of the correct intention, which is to provide the reader with an experience that is superior to the experiences the reader encounters in everyday life.

question: Have a friend with no talent for acting read your draft aloud in a flat monotone, as if the words had no meaning; wherever the emotion dies, rewrite so the words themselves carry it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What we learned with each stab of pain was that the words themselves and not the inflections supplied by the reader had to carry the emotion of the story.

question: Find the raw, pedestrian facts in your nonfiction and elaborate them with images, anecdotes, characterization, and writerly precision — borrow fiction’s techniques to bring the page alive.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The reader, soon bored, yearns for the images, anecdotes, characterization, and writerly precision that make informational writing come alive on the page. That is where the techniques of fiction can be so helpful to the nonfiction writer.

question: Audit your nonfiction for invention: you may make readers feel what happened, but you dare not invent what happened, cannot invent actions, and cannot guess what people were thinking.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It can make us feel what happened, but dares not invent what happened. Nonfiction can describe effectively what people do and thereby move us, but it cannot invent those actions. Nonfiction can report what people say, but it cannot guess what they were thinking.

question: Rewrite your opening so it arouses curiosity instead of answering everything up front — a reader who is sated by the first paragraph moves on to the next story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Today, the best of good journalists are arousing their readers’ curiosity in the first paragraph and seducing them into the rest of the story.

question: Before writing each scene, plan the reader’s adventure through it; after a respite away from it, revise with an editor’s steel gaze to see how the reader’s experience might be improved.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: But the less experienced writer can plan the reader’s adventure before he writes each scene, and in revising that scene after a respite away from it, with the steel gaze of an editor he can see how the reader’s experience might be improved.

question: Practice your craft deliberately, as ballet dancers, pianists, and actors do — only writers expect to achieve mastery without practice.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: By practice one learns to use what one has understood. Only writers, it seems, expect to achieve some level of mastery without practice.

question: Make the writing a good experience for both partners — you and the reader — and stop ignoring the reader’s pleasure in the exchange.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It has to be a good experience for both partners, the writer and the reader, and it is a source of distress to me to observe how frequently writers ignore the pleasure of their partners.

question: Scan your draft for sameness — the same sentence shapes and rhythms, like a blue suit with a blue shirt and blue tie — and rewrite for variety.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: “Your suit is blue,” he said. “Your shirt is blue, your tie is blue. That’s what’s wrong with your writing.”

question: Rewrite the passage so it evokes sensation in the reader — not the fact that it’s raining, but the feeling of being rained upon.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As E. L. Doctorow once put it, “Good writing is supposed to evoke sensation in the reader, not the fact that it’s raining, but the feeling of being rained upon.”

question: Take a statistic in your draft and refocus it on one individual the reader can see — lose the numbers and focus on the person, as 1,400 homeless people become the man on the 88th Street bench.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: TRADITIONAL NONFICTION: New York City has more than 1,400 homeless people. BETTER NONFICTION: The man who has laid claim to the bench on the corner of 88th Street and Park Avenue is one of New York City’s 1,400 homeless people.

question: Read a few chapters of a transient bestseller and study its mistakes — you can learn more from the painfully bad than from masterpieces, and it sharpens your editorial eye.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I learned more from the painfully bad than from the few remarkable plays that kept me enthralled. Today, I urge my students once they have begun to master craft, to read a few chapters of John Grisham’s The Firm, or some other transient bestseller, to see what they can learn from the mistakes of writers who don’t heed the precise meanings of the words they use.

question: Treat expert criticism as something to endure and perfect against: no matter how advanced your career, criticism cuts to the quick, so keep working to challenge it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It took some time for me to learn the other lesson, that a writer, shy or not, needs a tough skin, for no matter how advanced one’s experience and career, expert criticism cuts to the quick, and one learns to endure and to perfect, if for no other reason than to challenge the pain-maker.

question: Take an incident you witnessed or remember and write not what happened but what might have happened — let it be a taking-off point, not a report.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For the story writer, witnessing—or remembering—incidents in life must be more than an act of reporting. It is the taking-off point not of what happened, but of what might have happened.

question: Check that your work does its job with you absent — the writing alone must act on the reader’s mind and emotions, because the writer is dispensable and the work must do the job.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In fact when the writer finishes his work, he can vanish from the earth and his book will continue to affect the reader’s mind and emotions. The writer becomes dispensable. The work must do the job.

question: Find what your characters see or sense in silence but never say, and write the words that reveal what would otherwise be blinked away.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Wilder taught me that what a writer deals with is the unspoken, what people see or sense in silence.

question: Characterize your protagonist through action in the opening, set up the conflict, and involve the reader in the character's emotional state.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The writer, Anne Mudgett, is using action to characterize. She is also setting up conflict between the narrator and Mason, and involving the reader in Shoshana's emotional state.

question: Introduce action into your first sentence — guards rushing to the scene — to help dramatize it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did you note also that the introduction of action—the security guards rushing to the scene—helped dramatize that first sentence?

question: Use your first sentence to announce your theme dramatically — 'The two most successful creations of American movies are the gangster and the Westerner: men with guns.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A first sentence can be used to announce a theme dramatically.

question: Convey a person's attitude through a visual detail instead of the cliché — show the head held high rather than saying he was 'maintaining his innocence.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This one conveys the attitude of the person without the cliché of 'maintaining his innocence.'

question: Search your draft for a good lead buried elsewhere and bring it forward to replace a less worthy beginning, so the reader is turned on to reading the whole.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In my first reading of nonfiction I sometimes find that a good lead is buried elsewhere in the draft. Brought forward it can replace a less worthy beginning and help ensure that a reader will be turned on to reading the whole.

question: Open with candor — something you would rather the world not know, that you might keep secret if you were not a writer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Can candor at the beginning help your article, perhaps something you would rather the world not know that you might keep secret if you were not a writer?

question: Make the character you open with quickly more interesting than most of the people who surround us in life, so the reader becomes involved in that life rather than merely savoring your language.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The reader who savors language can be aroused by the author's language, but that arousal won't last unless the reader also becomes involved in the life of a character who is quickly more interesting than most of the people who surround us in life.

question: Give the character in your first scene something he wants badly, and let the reader feel it early — we are immediately interested in a character who wants something badly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As readers, we are immediately interested in a character who wants something badly.

question: Open with characterization — a personality trait or predicament — instead of incident, and let it seize the reader's attention on its own.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note that all of Bellow's beginnings except Henderson seize the attention of the reader by characterization, which we get soon enough.

question: Find a detail in your first sentence whose description clashes with what happens — a deadly bridge called 'the finest' — so the reader wants to know what happened and why.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: But the key to arousing our interest is in the words 'finest bridge.' Bridges deteriorate. Many are hazardous. But this bridge that suddenly hurtled five people to their death was 'the finest.' We want to know what happened, and why.

question: Pack your first paragraph with concrete detail while introducing the main characters and the tension between them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That first long paragraph introduces the two main characters, the narrator and his victim. Note the amount of concrete detail.

question: Replace flat intensifiers with a concrete, original metaphor that conveys degree — 'pain without pity or horizon' rather than 'endless' — and let contrast sharpen it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note the use of metaphoric language, 'pain without pity or horizon.' How much stronger 'horizon' is than 'endless' would be. Note also 'galactic sweep,' an effective and original way of conveying degree. Contrast helps.

question: Enhance the hard fact in your opening with contrast, resonance, and surprise — 'In death, life.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He enhances the hard fact with contrast, resonance, and surprise. In death, life.

question: Choose the word that identifies your lead subject by what creates contrast with the event — 'grandmother' rather than her name — to make the difference work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did you note the word 'grandmother'? The reporter could have said her name, Alice Hackmeyer, instead, but it wouldn't have created the same contrast with the event as 'grandmother' does.

question: Pair a shocking desire with a countervailing force that complicates it — the repugnance of having to touch the person you want to strangle — so the reader feels the tension rather than just the shock.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The narrator wants to perform an act that is taboo and punishable, but what causes the reaction of the reader is the countervailing force, the repugnance at having to touch the person you want to strangle.

question: Reframe a flat factual lead to turn on the engine of curiosity — find the surprising measure in it, like the family that took fourteen years to move two blocks.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It took fourteen years for the Buschkowski family to move two blocks. That lead turns on the engine of curiosity, the driving force that gets readers beyond the first sentences.

question: Cut the abstractions from your opening — a version bloated with abstractions is boring to read no matter how accurate.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is not the brevity that counts but the fact that the Huxley version is bloated with abstractions and is boring to read.

question: Stop cramming who, what, when, where, and why into your first paragraph — naked facts are not enough to invite the reader into the rest of the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When the journalist crams who, what, when, where, and why into the first paragraph, how can he hold the reader's attention for the whole of what he has written? Naked facts are frequently not enough to invite a reader's attention to the rest of the story.

question: Cut any opening that describes a happy, harmonious, conflict-free state — 'a wonderful couple' who never argued — the worst possible way to start a story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The worst possible way to start a story is with something like 'They were a wonderful couple. He loved her and she loved him. They never argued.'

question: Cut the melodramatic, clichéd phrases from your account — a head dropping 'like a rock,' a back heaving convulsively — they turn the writing unbelievable.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The account turns melodramatic. The toll taker's head drops like a cliché, her back 'heaves convulsively'—and unbelievably.

question: Check your lead for straining-for-effect analogies and cut the ones where the reader can feel you trying too hard to lure him into dull material.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In enhancing journalism with the techniques of fiction, caution is required. It's easy to overdo the attempt at analogy. One can feel the New York Times reporter straining for effect in the following attempt to lure the reader into the sometimes dull material of a House of Representatives vote:

question: Open your piece with a surprising image and hold back the subject's identity for a delayed reveal — 'several hundred bearers of a strategic commodity... They are goats.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An easy way to interest the reader at the outset is by the use of surprise.

question: Study the first few pages of the books that have pleased you most and locate the exact place where the engine turns on — where you could not put the book down.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is a useful exercise for writers to spend time in their libraries at home or in public libraries, looking at the first few pages of the books that have pleased them most in order to find the exact place where the engine turns on, where the reader will not want to put the book down.

question: Find the point at which the reader makes the decision not to put the book down — the engine — and move it as close to the top of page one as you can.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The 'engine' of both fiction and nonfiction is the point at which the reader makes the decision not to put the book down. The engine should start in the first three pages, the closer to the top of page one the better.

question: Let metaphor and colorful exaggeration enliven your opening sentences to tempt the reader on, so long as the excess does not mislead anyone about what happened.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note the colorful exaggeration that strays from strict fact. The street asphalt was not literally crushed into powder ('pulverized') but broken into slabs and pieces.

question: Move your most interesting fact from the first sentence to the last of the opening paragraph, where it thrusts the reader forward into the next paragraph and establishes tone.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The fact in the last sentence of the paragraph would normally have gone into the first sentence. It was put last for two reasons. It was given the job of thrusting the reader forward into the next paragraph. More important was the establishment of tone.

question: Craft your nonfiction facts so they touch the reader's emotions — information sticks best when it is crafted that way.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Information sticks best when it is crafted to touch the reader's emotions.

question: Make your first sentence deliver several facts at once, each of which raises a question the reader wants answered — age, situation, regularity, and the interruption to come.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That first sentence tells us the narrator is old, that he is in bed with someone of the same sex, that this is a regular event in his life, and the event this day is being interrupted by a visit from an archbishop!

question: Ask of your first sentence: does it convey an interesting personality or an action we want to know more about, and can it be made more intriguing by introducing something unusual, shocking, or surprising?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are questions you can ask yourself about your own first sentence: Does it convey an interesting personality or an action that we want to know more about? Can you make your first sentence more intriguing by introducing something unusual, something shocking perhaps, or something that will surprise the reader?

question: Revise your first three pages so they arouse the reader's interest enough to quarantine him from distraction for the several hours the book demands from him.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thereafter, whenever an author told me that his novel really got going on page ten or twenty or thirty, I had to pass on the news that his book in all likelihood was doomed unless he could revise it so that the first three pages aroused the reader's interest enough to quarantine him from distraction for the several hours the book demanded from him.

question: Find the one word in your opening that characterizes your character in a flash — 'ferret' — and make sure that word is doing the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Most writers quickly come up with the correct answer: 'ferret.' It characterizes sixteen-year-old Sammy in a flash.

question: Check your opening: does it immerse the reader in heightened experience, emotional or intellectual, more rewarding than the life around him, or does it bore him toward the death end of the line?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Successful writing immerses the reader in heightened experience—emotional, intellectual, or both—more rewarding than the life around him.

question: Invert a familiar phrase in your first sentence — 'Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent' — to produce two attention-getters in half a sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We don't think of judging saints. And Orwell inverts the usual 'innocent until proven guilty,' producing two attention-getters in half a sentence.

question: Run your draft first paragraph through the checklist: does the first sentence trigger curiosity, what will the reader see in it, have you focused on an individual with a visible characteristic doing or saying something, and is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your first sentence trigger curiosity to make the reader want to continue? What will the reader see in that first sentence? Have you focused on an individual? Have you given us a visible characteristic of that individual? Have you portrayed the individual doing or saying something? Is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

question: End an ominous sentence with a run of short, monosyllabic words to strengthen the feeling, as in 'the next snow fell.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'Daring death' is an omen. And the rhythm of the words at the end of the sentence is designed to strengthen the ominous feeling in 'the next snow fell.'

question: Position your narrator in a relationship to the main character that itself raises questions the reader wants answered — will he keep putting up with this person, will the person get what he is after?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The fact that the narrator is Sammy's boss also piques the reader's curiosity. Will the narrator continue to put up with Sammy's drive? Will Sammy get fired? Will Sammy succeed, and if so at what and how will he do it?

question: Treat your nonfiction opening with the same goal as a fiction writer: spark the reader's interest sufficiently to engage him in reading the rest.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: At the beginning of a piece of nonfiction, the goal of the writer is the same as that of a writer of fiction: to spark the reader's interest sufficiently to engage him in reading the rest.

question: Mint a novel comparison for a familiar object — four giant Oscars 'like sullen art deco Nazis' — and trim the hedging that weakens it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A novel comparison also makes a good hook: At the Academy Awards, the entrance to the Shrine Civil Auditorium is flanked by four giant Oscars quite, or so it seems to me, like sullen art deco Nazis. The sentence might have been improved by omitting 'or so it seems to me' but the comparison is startling and strong nevertheless.

question: Instead of a loud hook, seduce the reader leisurely by planting omens that something is going to happen, building apprehension before the action starts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are, however, more leisurely ways to seduce the reader, through omens.

question: Check your opening paragraph against the three goals: does it excite the reader's curiosity about a character or a relationship, introduce a setting, and lend resonance to the story? Revise until the first is strongly at work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The ideal goals of an opening paragraph are: 1. To excite the reader's curiosity, preferably about a character or a relationship. 2. To introduce a setting. 3. To lend resonance to the story.

question: Replace the flat, abstract name for a character trait with an original, concrete word — 'thirsty' instead of 'ambitious.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'thirsty,' an original way of saying Sammy was hungry, meaning ambitious.

question: Try opening with pseudo-candor — a disclaimer that does the opposite of what the reader expects and is a cover-up for a fault — as effective as candor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Both examples entice with a slight surprise because they do the opposite of what we expect. Both seem to be disclaimers. Each is a cover-up for a fault. They both might be characterized as pseudo-candor, which can be as effective as candor.

question: Try a quiet first sentence that intrigues through implication rather than shock — 'She might have been waiting for her lover.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Here's a quieter—yet intriguing—opening sentence by one of the century's grand masters, Graham Greene, from an early (1935) novel, England Made Me. She might have been waiting for her lover.

question: Repeat a key word in your lead to underscore the detail that matters — repetition for effect increases the dramatic impact of what's being described.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did you note that repeating the word 'umbrella' underscored Sorbino's walking out with someone else's purse? That technique—repetition for effect—increases the dramatic impact of what's being described.

question: Start with a scene the reader can see, and begin that scene as close to its climax as is feasible to involve the reader quickly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your aim is publication, your best bet is to start with a scene that the reader can see. Where do you start that scene? As close to its climax as is feasible if your aim is to involve the reader quickly.

question: Keep a conventional opening if you like, but season it with just enough that is unconventional to rouse the reader's curiosity — a narrator who is 'naked at the moment and talking into the dark.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A craftsman like Cheever will season even the most conventional beginning with just enough that is unconventional to rouse the reader's curiosity.

question: Open with an injunction of secrecy or a promise of revelation — 'You must not tell anyone what I am about to tell you' — that makes the reader want what is being withheld.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'You must not tell anyone,' my mother said, 'what I am about to tell you.'

question: Give your subject a small observed action — ducking his head — to picture him, the way a novelist would.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Head-ducking is not much of an action, but a reporter who is a keen observer of small detail would have the advantage of the novelist in picturing Brucell and giving him an action, however small, like ducking his head:

question: Introduce sound into your lead — the meeting room 'to loud applause' — to make it better.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: George Brucell, a tall man, had to duck his head as the chairman ushered him into the meeting room to loud applause. Better because of the introduction of sound.

question: Open by spotlighting a single individual, characterized however briefly, performing an eccentric and somehow beautiful act — an excellent way of involving the reader's emotions.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Burns helps us see a besieged city by focusing on a single individual performing an eccentric and somehow beautiful act. Spotlighting an individual who is characterized, however briefly, is an excellent way of involving the reader's emotions.

question: Plant an early surprise that unsettles the reader's expectation — a twist on who the speaker is or on what you led them to assume.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Our curiosity is aroused when a surprise unsettles our expectation.

question: Pair an unexpected subject with an unexpected attitude in your first sentence — 'I have long been an admirer of the octopus' — to be both surprising and a touch amusing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I have long been an admirer of the octopus. Octopus? Admirer? That opening is both surprising and a touch amusing.

question: Introduce a visual element into your lead — a head held high, trouble keeping his eyes on the judge — to perk it up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A visual element can almost always be introduced to perk up a lead.

question: Open with a visual parallel that connects two incongruous elements — the mourners in scuffed white sneakers at the viewing of a draftsman of shoes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Andy Warhol, draftsman of shoes, is dead, and the people viewing his remains are mostly wearing scuffed white sneakers. Note the visual parallel.

question: Present your narrator's core problem through a concrete visual image rather than an abstract statement of it — show the wrong parents, don't say 'I was born to the wrong parents.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That visual opening presents the narrator's problem—the wrong parents!—in an attention-grabbing way. How abstract the beginning would have sounded had the author started, 'I was born to the wrong parents.'

question: Check your action sequences: anything that is mere motion, things merely happening, replace with action, which is what people do and say.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In fiction, action consists of what people do and say. Hemingway said it perfectly: “Never mistake motion for action.”

question: Re-read your scene for the sound of your own voice and cut it: direct what happens onstage, but never appear as one of the actors.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Writers are directors of what transpires on the other side of the glass. They are not one of the actors.
