question: Build resonance into a scene so it carries what the moment means beyond the visible action—the difference between ordinary and extraordinary writing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The difference between ordinary nonfiction and extraordinary writing, as in Mattingly, is often in the resonance:

question: Make a person come alive by rendering their appearance with one specific detail.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The best way to make a person come alive is by rendering the person’s appearance with some specific detail.

question: Vitalize a person in a sentence or two by selecting one unusual characteristic, drawing on animals, fish, birds, insects, or plants for the image.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Novelists learn to provide vitality to minor characters in a sentence or two, usually by selecting one characteristic that is unusual. Our dictionaries are full of animals, fish, birds, and insects that can be used in the characterization of people.

question: Replace a vague factual image like “dressed all in black” with particulars that carry feeling, not just the fact.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A layman might describe a man as being dressed all in black. The image is vague, it gets the fact across, but not the feeling. It could have been written by anybody.

question: Conjure a mental snapshot so private you wouldn’t carry it in your wallet — something you wouldn’t want a paramedic, neighbor, closest friend, or family member to find.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I ask the author to think of a snapshot of something so private he wouldn’t carry it in his wallet because if he were in an accident, he wouldn’t want a paramedic to find it. The snapshot we’re looking for is one the writer wouldn’t want his neighbor or closest friend to see. Not even a family member. Especially not a family member.

question: Expect your first draft to be flawed and to need your editorial skills. Instead of despairing over how awful it reads, treat revision as your second chance to fix it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you review what you’ve written and exclaim, “Oh my God, this is awful!” you’ll only dispirit yourself. The experienced writer knows his first draft will be flawed, that he will get a chance to employ his editorial skills in fixing it.

question: Look closely at what you write and test each word and phrase for both accuracy and necessity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In this chapter, we’ve learned to look closely at what we write, to test each word and phrase both for accuracy and necessity.

question: Where one adjective cannot create the specific image, keep a second adjective or an adverb modifying the adjective, as in “heavily pregnant.”

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Sometimes two adjectives or an adverb modifying the adjective are necessary to create a specific image: Meryl Streep stood the way a heavily pregnant woman will, in two motions, out of the chair and then up.

question: Test each adjective for necessity: if removing it would mislead the reader, as removing “right” would in “His right eye kept blinking,” keep it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An adjective that is a necessity. Example: “His right eye kept blinking.” If you didn’t keep “right,” it might sound as if you were talking about a one-eyed man.

question: Sweep out your adverb clusters and shorten your sentences; pace improves from both moves at once.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The pace is improved not only by eliminating five adverbs, but also by shortening the sentences.

question: Cut adverbs whose meaning the verb already connotes—scribbling implies hurry, so “hurriedly” goes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Why get rid of “hurriedly”? Because scribbling connotes hurry.

question: Keep paired adverbs when each conveys a distinct meaning you intend, as “heartily” and “happily” each carry their own connotation.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He ate heartily, happily. “Heartily” connotes eating a lot, “happily” connotes taking pleasure. If it is the author’s intention to convey both meanings, the adverbs should be retained.

question: Test each adverb against two keep-rules: does it supply necessary information, or does it help the reader visualize the precise image? Cut the rest.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Keep an adverb that supplies necessary information. Example: “He tried running faster and fell.” If he’s already running, you must keep “faster.”

question: Cut empty structural fillers like “an” and “one” in “This idea is an interesting one”; “This idea is interesting” is stronger.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The flab words are “an” and “one.”

question: At your chapter endings, cut sentences that are excessively sentimental or too abstract, leaving the reader with a concrete emotion instead.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In revising, I thought the sentence “What does a mother do with her love?” excessively sentimental. And “Why did God do nothing?” was too abstract to leave the reader with a suitable emotion at the end of the chapter. I cut both sentences.

question: Replace clichés—tired, overused word pairs like “huffing and puffing”—with the single word that carries the meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It’s the “huffing and puffing” that spoils the sentence because that phrase is a cliché, a tired, overused, familiar conjunction of words.

question: When you cut one of two paired adjectives, drop the comma with it—commas tend to slow the reading process.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Quite apart from eliminating one out of six words, the comma goes too, and commas tend to slow the reading process.

question: Replace bland paired adjectives with a single adjective that piques the reader’s curiosity—curious, strange, eerie—one that makes them want to know why.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Examining your adjectives provides an opportunity to see if you could possibly invoke the reader’s curiosity with an adjective that is better than either one you now have.

question: When a whole sentence adds nothing, cut the entire sentence—the deletion strengthens what is left and steps up the pace.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I cut the entire middle sentence, which didn’t add anything. The deletion strengthened what was left and stepped up the pace:

question: Cut the flab from your text: removing unnecessary words improves pace and strengthens the body of what remains.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Flab-cutting is one of the best means for improving the pace of both fiction and nonfiction. When eliminated, the loss of fat has the welcome side effect of strengthening the body of remaining text.

question: Find and delete every “very” and “quite” that crept into your first draft.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The easiest ones to dispense with are “very” and “quite.” Word processing programs make the process simple. Find and delete all the verys, and quites that crept into your first draft.

question: When two images convey the same thing, cut one—duplicated images make the reader conscious of the craft instead of the effect, and the pace speeds up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Two images that convey the same thing make the reader conscious of the images instead of letting the reader experience the effect. And by cutting one of the two, the pace speeds up.

question: When a general clause restates a more specific one, delete the general clause—it says the same thing twice.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The first clause is general and familiar. “It was a time of purest humiliation” is more specific. All you have to do is delete the words “a dreadful situation” and you have a more specific sentence that doesn’t say the same thing twice.

question: Don’t apply the one-plus-one rule to a conscious piling-up of words for effect—intentional piling adds force; accidental repetition diminishes it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The “one plus one” guideline does not apply to a conscious piling-up of words for effect.

question: When two sentences say the same thing, cut the one that weakens the setup—keep the short first sentence so the specific image lands.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You could have eliminated either of the first two sentences. My preference would be to eliminate the second sentence because the short first sentence sets up the effective last sentence better:

question: When you cut excess verbiage, keep words that help the reader visualize the precise image you are trying to fashion, even when their meaning is implied.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In cutting excess verbiage, keep words that help the reader visualize the precise image you are trying to fashion.

question: Find two sentences where the second merely names what the first already implies, and merge them into one faster sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the moment of illumination, though, he saw him. Buster Devonne was counting his money.

question: Cut your narrator’s generalization about what he has just shown—the specific scene is enough, and the generalization distracts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The narrator’s generalization of what he sees is distracting. In the editing, the second sentence should come out.

question: Cut adjectives that state the obvious or add nothing to the image—“quaint and white” weakens “an old man in sculptured soap.”

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We usually think of soap as white unless a color is indicated. And “quaint” means “odd in a pleasing way” or “oldfashioned.” Neither definition really helps the image in this context. “An old man in sculptured soap” is strong. “An old man in sculptured soap, quaint and white,” is weaker.

question: Apply the formula “one plus one equals a half”: saying the same thing over and over minimizes its impact, so cut the redundancy.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I’ve been teaching my strange formula “One plus one equals a half” for a long time. It has been of value even to the most talented and successful of writers.

question: Become your own editor: publishers do far less line editing than they used to, so catching redundancy is the writer’s job.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The hard fact is that editors do a lot less line editing than they used to. If a novel requires a lot of line editing, it is less likely to be taken on by a publisher, who has to consider the cost of editing. Which is why is it incumbent upon writers to become, in effect, their own editors.

question: Cut redundancies where one term includes the other—“my parents, Mom and Dad”—and keep one or the other, not both.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Who else might her parents be besides “Mom and Dad”? The script writer should have kept one or the other, not both.

question: Never choose between adjectives arbitrarily. Use words for their precise meaning in context; that is the mark of a good writer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In addition to eliminating unnecessary words, I am focusing on using words for their precise meaning, which is the mark of a good writer.

question: Cut words that restate what another word already encompasses, like “private and public” before “life,” and drop phrases that add unnecessary information.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The word “life” encompasses private and public. “Over the last fifteen years” provided unnecessary information that weakened the sentence.

question: Strip every adjective and adverb from your manuscript, then readmit only the few that survive careful testing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The quickest way of increasing the pace of a manuscript and strengthening it at the same time is to remove all adjectives and adverbs and then readmit the necessary few after careful testing.

question: Be as tough on yourself in eliminating unnecessary words as an editor would be—the best writers are the toughest on themselves.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Be as tough on yourself in eliminating unnecessary words as you think I might be if I were editing your manuscript. The best writers of the hundreds I’ve dealt with over the years were also the toughest on themselves.

question: Find every place where you used two adjectives with a single noun and eliminate one of them, keeping the more concrete or more visual adjective.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The more concrete adjective is the one to keep. Or the one that makes the image more visual.

question: When two adverbs modify one verb, try eliminating both—the unadorned verb is direct and picks up the pace.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You could take out either. “She really cared for him” is okay. “She truly cared for him” is okay too. But best of all is “She cared for him.” It is direct, and picks up the pace.

question: Compile your own list of flab words—“however,” “almost,” “perhaps,” “there is”—and sweep your text for each one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Certain words frequently constitute flab and can be eliminated: “however,” “almost,” “entire,” “successive,” “respective,” “perhaps,” “always,” “there is.” Each writer can compile a list of his own, words he uses from time to time that contribute nothing but flab to a text.

question: Write your story so it seems to be happening now, no matter when it is set.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Ideally, all fiction should seem to be happening now.

question: Read your flashback and judge whether it interrupts the reader's experience of the present story. The reader wants the ride, not a look at the machinery.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Therefore, the art of writing flashbacks is to avoid interrupting the reader's experience. ... The reader doesn't want to see your chains and pulleys, he just wants the ride.

question: Rewrite your flashback as a scene with characters in conflict, however short it is.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A true flashback, however short, is a scene, preferably with characters in conflict.

question: Cut the flashback if it doesn't markedly enhance the present story. If it isn't important to the story, you may not really need it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A flashback must illuminate the present story in an important way. Otherwise, why bother? If it doesn't enhance the present story markedly, you may not really need it.

question: Rewrite the flashback as an immediate scene the reader witnesses, depicted exactly as the present story would be — not an offstage narrative summary.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Whenever possible, the flashback should be an immediate scene rather than an offstage narrative summary. The reader needs to witness the flashback rather than be told about what happened. A good flashback is a scene that is depicted exactly as it would be in the present story except for how it is introduced and how the present story is rejoined.

question: Slip into your flashback quickly and unobtrusively so the reader never sees it coming and doesn't skip pages.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The object is to make the transition to the flashback as unobtrusive as possible. Slipping into the flashback quickly avoids the risk of the impatient reader skipping pages because he sees the flashback coming before it grips him.

question: Make the first sentence of your flashback arresting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The first sentence of a flashback needs to be arresting.

question: Purge every "had" and "then" from your flashback and write it in the straight past tense of your present scenes — "I remembered", not "I had been remembering".

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: "Had" is the number-one villain. It spoils more flashbacks than any other word. Most fiction is written in the straight past tense. When writing flashbacks, as quickly as possible use the same tense you're using for the present scenes. That means in almost all cases the straight past tense, not the variants. Instead of saying, "I had been remembering ...", say "I remembered ..."

question: Open your flashback with dialogue early, even if the flashback is short — dialogue is always an immediate scene.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In starting a flashback, your aim is to get into an immediate scene as soon as possible. Since dialogue is always in immediate scene, one way of handling flashbacks is to use dialogue early. What most writers don't realize is that you can use dialogue even if the flashback is short.

question: Introduce your flashback by seguing from the present scene into the past as inconspicuously as possible, rather than announcing the shift directly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can go into a flashback directly or segue into it. ... I prefer the segue into a flashback to the more direct method, moving from the present scene to a scene in the past inconspicuously.

question: Conclude your flashback with a line space, a time marker like "One week later ...", or dialogue that restarts the present scene.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can use a line space (four blank lines) to mark the passage of time and restart the present scene after the line space. Or you can begin a new paragraph with "One week later ..." Or you can restart the present scene with dialogue: "Last week you didn't talk this way."

question: Let your character's thoughts, including thoughts of the past, interrupt the present scene to enrich the character and give the scene texture.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: While flashbacks are to be avoided whenever possible, the flashback thought can be immensely useful in enriching both a character and a scene. In life our thoughts interrupt us all the time. ... Thoughts give texture to life and also to novels.

question: Build any past material that exceeds quick thoughts in an ongoing scene into a flashback scene that stands on its own — not a narrative of what happened elsewhere.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If the flashback element is to consist of more than quick thoughts in an ongoing scene, the writer must be certain to create a flashback scene that stands on its own to avoid the flashback becoming a narrative of something that happened elsewhere.

question: Fashion a flashback to increase suspense: insert it into a long confrontation scene so it postpones the outcome.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Flashbacks normally decrease suspense, but they can be fashioned to increase suspense. To heighten the suspense of that confrontation, I inserted three flashbacks into the scene, remembered by Nick, designed to increase the suspense by postponing the outcome of the confrontation.

question: Rewrite the background information as present dialogue so the reader witnesses a dramatic scene now and you eliminate the need for a flashback.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You've just seen how information can be conveyed in present dialogue in such a way that the reader is witnessing a dramatic scene that takes place in the present, thus eliminating the need for a flashback.

question: Convey the background the reader needs through a character's silent thoughts during a present scene instead of a flashback.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thoughts can accomplish the same purpose. ... Tommy has said absolutely nothing. We've been privy to his thoughts. And we've got the background we need right in the foreground.

question: Give the reader knowledge of your character before the crisis arrives — you have to know the people in the car before you see the crash.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You have to know the people in the car before you see the car crash. Shirley's flashback thoughts, added to her thoughts in the present, are how the reader gets to know Shirley and begins to want her not to jump.

question: Do a focused reading of your manuscript as a hunter on assignment, hunting for specific errors and omissions rather than reading as a reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you’ve considered those questions and fixed whatever needed fixing, it may be time for a focused reading, by which I mean a reading of your manuscript in which you read not as a reader but as a hunter for specific errors and omissions as if on assignment to do so.

question: Track the objects in your scene: when a character orders coffee, the coffee must appear — rewrite scenes where a prop vanishes between request and delivery.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
Coffee? Yes, he said, black. She disappeared and returned with a cup and saucer.

The coffee itself was presumably forgotten by the author.

question: Borrow the candor of another: quote someone else’s daring words — pass the candor chalice — to make the candid point yourself.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Vidal, who has never wanted for vitriol much less candor, begins one piece about Tennessee Williams by passing the candor chalice to Williams, whom he quotes saying, “I particularly like New York on hot summer nights when all the ... uh, superfluous people are off the streets.” Borrowing the candor of another has been useful to Joan Didion also.

question: Know that as a nonfiction writer you are more exposed than the novelist, who hides a little under the presumption that he is making things up — dare anyway.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The novelist has it easier. He hides a little—just a little—under the presumption that he is making things up. The nonfiction writer who dares to dare is more exposed.

question: Distinguish forthrightness from sensationalism: what your writing requires is honesty of a kind that gets self-suppressed by the public, not tabloid shock.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It should be evident by now that forthrightness doesn’t involve sensationalism suitable for the exploitation tabloids. What it requires is honesty of a kind that gets selfsuppressed by the public.

question: Find the one concrete incident in your material that can serve as the fulcrum of your piece and build the essay around it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As Pemberton was drying one of the Baccarat glasses, it shattered in her hand, a happy accident in that she used it as the fulcrum of her piece.

question: Take the oath to write nothing inoffensive: the success of an article or nonfiction book rests on your courage in revealing normally unspoken things about yourself or your society.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A long time ago I took an oath never to write anything inoffensive. The single characteristic that most makes a difference in the success of an article or nonfiction book is the author’s courage in revealing normally unspoken things about himself or his society.

question: Elaborate the hidden reality of your own work: write about what actually happens in your field — its normally private, unspoken acts — with precision, clarity, grace, and candor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He does what no surgeon has done before, with precision, clarity, grace, imagination, and candor:

question: Put what you actually think into the text: overcome your natural reluctance to say the things you think — fig leaves have no place on the minds of the best writers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Yes, after overcoming their natural reluctance to say the things they think. Fig leaves have no place on either the bodies or the minds of the best writers.

question: Rewrite toward the unspeakable: what makes writing at its best interesting is your willingness to say things that people don’t ordinarily say.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What makes writing at its best interesting is the writer’s willingness to broach the unspeakable, to say things that people don’t ordinarily say.

question: Give your hero faults and your villain charm: the hero’s faults bring him to life, and the villain’s charm is the honey with which he lures the innocent.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt imbue thy heroes with faults and thy villains with charm, for it is the faults of the hero that bring forth his life, just as the charm of the villain is the honey with which he lures the innocent.

question: When a word’s meaning is fuzzy to you, stop and ask what it precisely means — “human” is not “humane” — and replace words chosen off the top of your head out of speed.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the best of newspapers the best of journalists are usually forced to write quickly“off the top of the head” is the convenient expression—and that’s where an imprecise use of “human” comes from: speed and a minimum of thought, for surely both experienced authors of the Schwarzkopf biography know better.

question: Use immediate scenes wherever you can in your nonfiction, and put your first immediate scene on page one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Most important, the nonfiction writer who learns to use immediate scenes wherever he can will also find a dramatic improvement in the readability of his work. The ideal place for your first immediate scene is on page one.

question: Infect your reader with anxiety, stress, and tension, for the conditions they deplore in life they relish in fiction.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt infect thy reader with anxiety, stress, and tension, for those conditions that he deplores in life he relishes in fiction.

question: Replace every approximate word with the precisely right word: delight in le mot juste and never let the near-miss word pass in your own work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The serious writer is addicted to the precise meaning of words in his own work and admires le mot juste in the work of others. For him, the approximate word is never satisfactory, and he delights in the tools that enable him to be as precise as possible.

question: When you want to convey an emotion, search for words that evoke it — “lilting house” rather than the direct, obvious “happy house.”

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A poor poet might have written “happy house,” which is direct and obvious. The “lilting house” evokes the happiness.

question: Write characters understood in depth, engaged in activities resonant with the ambiguities and stresses of life, so that they persist in the reader’s mind after the reading is over.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The literary novelist is concerned primarily with character understood in depth and engaged in activities that are resonant with the ambiguities and stresses of life. The richness of the best literary fiction is derived primarily from the creation of characters who will persist in the reader’s mind after the reading experience is over.

question: When your scene is literary rather than commercial fiction, make the characters' differing scripts more subtle instead of broadly clashing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This technique works well for scenes in both commercial and literary fiction, with the scripts in literary fiction differing more subtly.

question: When you devise a locale for a scene, choose a closed environment — it will invariably increase the tension — and think of that locale when you are first imagining your characters.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When devising a locale for a scene, it always pays to give a few moments thought to the possibility of choosing a closed environment. It will invariably increase the tension of the scene. The ideal time to think of that locale is when you are first imagining your characters.

question: Give the animal in your story a distinctive particularity, as you would a human character, and tie that characteristic to the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It takes skill to make an animal believable as a character, and the best method is to give it a particularity just as you would a human character, a distinctive characteristic and preferably one that relates to the story—for instance a cat that jumps up into the lap of everyone but the person who loves it.

question: Give the animal in your story a clear want of its own instead of making it a passive recipient of the human characters' wants.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
Also, it is important that the animal have a clear want of its own and

not be merely the passive recipient of human wants.

question: Cut the mechanical description of sexual activity from your love scene; it will not arouse readers and fails to evoke a loving experience between people.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Some people, and consequently some writers, have never learned that mechanical description of sexual activity does not usually arouse readers who are no longer adolescents.

question: Before writing your love scene, consider what the reader is feeling at each moment; the primary erogenous zone is in the reader's head.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The main flaw in most love scenes is similar to that of the main flaws in all other scenes: the reader’s emotions have been insufficiently considered by the writer. The primary erogenous zone is in the head, and that’s where the reader experiences writing.

question: Consider your love scene from the point of view of each partner even when writing from one character's disciplined point of view, so the reader understands the relationship better than either lover does.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This can be accomplished if the writer considers the love scene from the point of view of each of the characters even when writing from the disciplined point of view of one of them. The reader needs to understand the relationship between the lovers better than either of the lovers do.

question: Build your love scene from tension and tenderness: postpone the consummation as long as credibility permits and keep the likely outcome hidden from the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The two most essential ingredients in love scenes are tension and tenderness. A crisis in the relationship or postponing lovemaking, keeping the lovers apart as long as credibility permits, generates tension. It’s a mistake to let the reader know early the likely outcome of the scene.

question: Rewrite your love scene so the attraction between the lovers seems new, even in a longstanding relationship; no love scene should repeat a familiar ritual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: No love scene should be the repetition of a familiar ritual. To sustain the reader’s interest in the outcome, the attraction should seem new even in a longstanding relationship.

question: Delay the consummation of your love scene and build anticipation through minutiae—small actions and details—while the possibility of contact hangs in the air.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The writer’s first temptation might be to let them in the house, to get on with it. But delay builds anticipation. It can be accomplished by minutiae:

question: Cut the sentimentality from your love scene—any emotion that is exaggerated or affected and obviously designed to win the reader's sympathy—and aim instead for a depth of feeling.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The writer invokes sentimentality when he elicits superficial emotions that are exaggerated, excessive, or affected, obviously designed to elicit the reader’s sympathy. Sentimentality in fiction usually comes across as patently insincere, mawkish, or maudlin, and should be avoided. A writer’s sensibility should be directed toward evoking a depth of feeling in the reader, not to fabricating superficial excesses of emotion on the page.

question: Consider putting both the gain and the loss of love in the same story; together they are doubly powerful.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The gain of love and the loss of love are powerful combustibles. It is doubly powerful to have both gain and loss of love in the same story.

question: Make each of your lovers vulnerable in a different way, and evoke the reader's feelings through what they say and do rather than telling the reader what they feel.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Keep in mind that you don’t want to tell the reader what they are feeling, but to evoke feelings in the reader as a result of what the young lovers say to each other and what they do. It helps to make each of them vulnerable in a different way.

question: Derive your love plot and what happens in your love scene from your characters' motivations; remind yourself that plot grows out of character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In plotting a love story, a writer must remind himself that plot grows out of character.

question: Give each of your lovers one thing that distinguishes their physical appearance, and a distinctive way of dressing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does each of your lovers have one thing that distinguishes his or her physical appearance from that of other people? Is there something distinctive in the way your lovers dress?

question: Search your love story for root conflicts based on character and upbringing, and add a surface crisis that increases the tension if your lovers are not already at a moment of crisis.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In devising a love story, search for the root conflicts based on character and upbringing, but also ferret out surface conflict by asking yourself if you have depicted your adult lovers at a moment of crisis. If not, can you add a crisis that will increase the tension of the relationship?

question: Ask whether your love story has enough friction between the lovers to hold the reader's interest, but not so much that the reader stops believing they are in love.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Whatever your plan, remember that if there is no friction between the lovers, there is no interest on the part of the reader. And if there is massive friction, will the reader be convinced that they are nevertheless in love?

question: Write ten brief exchanges of dialogue between two lovers that make the reader feel both that they are quarreling and that they are lovers, not ex-lovers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One exercise writers in my classes have found to be exceptionally beneficial is writing an exchange of ten lines of dialogue, alternating between two lovers. The object is to have the reader experience two things from the ten lines: that the characters are quarreling and that they are lovers (not ex-lovers).

question: Write your best scenes with more than one thing going on at a time, as in a quarrel that is unmistakably a lovers' exchange.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: But that is precisely the kind of thing a writer must do in the best of scenes, have more than one thing going on at a time.

question: For your older lovers, keep a hovering notion that they do not have all the time in the world, include the need for companionship, and add a touch that enhances the poignancy.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
In developing your love scene, is there a hovering notion that the lovers do not have all

the time in the world?

Have you included the need for companionship, often the most urgent need of older people?

Have you included touching or some other physical relationship that will enhance the poignancy?

question: Imagine your love scene from the perspective of each partner; if you are a man, give special thought to the woman's perspective, and if a woman, to the man's.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The key to writing an effective love scene is to imagine it from the perspective of each of the partners. If the writer is a woman, she should give special thought to the perspective of the man in the scene. If the writer is a man, he should give special thought to the perspective of the woman.

question: Enrich your love scene by having one of the participants gain an insight about the other person.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
A scene can also be enriched if either of the participants gains an insight about the

other person.

question: Plant a meaningful object before your love scene, keep it unnoticed until an important juncture, and let one lover's reaction to it turn the scene so the other must rekindle the relationship.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can place an object in the room that is meaningful to one or both lovers. If possible, plant the object before the love scene. Don’t let either of the lovers notice it until an important juncture in that scene, when one of them sees the object, turns off, and the other lover has to rekindle the relationship.

question: Introduce an unexpected misunderstanding that deepens the more one lover tries to clear it up, then bring in a third character who either worsens or resolves the impasse.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A tack you might consider is to have something unexpected happen that causes a misunderstanding. The more one of the lovers tries to clear up the misunderstanding, the deeper it gets. Make it seem that the impasse is unsurmountable. Then introduce a third character, who can make the impasse worse, or who can provide a way of clearing up the misunderstanding.

question: Interrupt your love scene with a significant thought or memory; it can be more effective than a loud external event.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: But note this. Though an action is the ideal interruption, a thought can also interrupt, particularly a significant thought or memory, and it can be a lot more effective than the local volcano blowing its top.

question: Write a poignant love scene in which the lovers never come close enough to touch; a love scene and a sex scene are not the same.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A love scene and a sex scene are not the same. A poignant love scene can be written with the lovers not coming close enough to touch.

question: Cut the multiple sexual acts from your erotic scene; a single act kept at bay and stretched out can have a marked erotic effect.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
The point to grasp is that the mere description of multiple sexual acts does little or nothing for the reader. A single act,

kept at bay, warmed to, stretched out, can have a marked erotic effect.

question: Before writing your erotic scene, be clear about the relationship between the couple and what the sexual intimacy accomplishes in your story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In preparing to write an erotic scene, the writer has to be clear about the relationship between the couple, and has to know what he is trying to accomplish in his story through the sexual intimacy.

question: Give every sexual encounter in your story a meaning for at least one of the characters, or it does not belong in the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Even a meaningless assignation has to have a meaning for at least one of the characters or it doesn’t belong in the story.

question: In your one-night stand scene, ask why each participant is doing this and how each reacts during and after, so the encounter conveys something about each character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A brief, not-to-be-repeated encounter has greater potential for a story than a meaningless copulation, but to have an important effect on the reader it, too, has to convey something about each character. Why is each of the participants doing this, and how does each of them react to the experience while it’s happening and afterward?

question: Write the sexual encounter that begins a love affair as a back-and-forth experience, not a straight line; let digressions that serve the scene heighten and extend it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Think of it as a back-and-forth experience and not a straight line. Each digression—if it doesn’t take the reader away from the fundamental goal of the scene—can heighten and extend the experience.

question: Have your character put himself down in a way that raises him in the reader's eyes; self-deprecation can signal insight and make him a more interesting lover.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When Thomassy puts himself down, he is actually raising himself in the reader’s eyes. The reader knows how tough and successful he is as a lawyer.

question: Write the tension of arousal in short sentence snippets, then render the breakthrough as one long breathless extended sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note that the scene consists of many short sentences. Then, the paragraph in which they move to the couch is long, almost all of it one extended sentence. The tension of arousal is handled with snippets. The breakthrough is written as breathless continuum.

question: For lovers who have made love before, add a surprise, the opposite of the expected, or an intrusion that stops the inevitable outcome.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Lovemaking between a couple that has made love before can be a more difficult task for the writer. Art imitates life. If the likely outcome is known to the participants, it removes an element of suspense. For the experienced writer it may mean creating a delay, or even an event or action that stops the inevitable. A scene between lovers experienced with each other can be helped by a surprise, the opposite of the expected, or an intrusion.

question: Break up any scene of continuous lovemaking with thoughts, actions, digressions, and delays pertinent to the story; list each character's concerns and make them different to maximize tension.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In writing any sexual episode, you have to guard against fashioning a scene of continuous lovemaking. It needs to be broken up by thoughts, actions, digressions, delays that are pertinent to the story. Toward that end, you may find it useful to make a list of each character’s concerns during the scene. To maximize tension, those concerns should be different.

question: Give each of your characters a different script for their love scene, as in the Actors Studio technique.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Keep the Actors Studio technique in mind by giving each of your characters a different script for their love scene.

question: As you revise your love scene, test each part of it for what you believe the reader is feeling at that moment.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you revise, test each part of the scene for what you believe the reader is feeling at that moment.

question: Rephrase the explicit moments in your love scene so the reader's imagination does the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You need to remind yourself until it becomes second nature that you are playing the emotions of an audience. In writing love scenes, you need to let the reader’s imagination do a lot of the work.

question: Replace violent or graphic moments in your love scenes with small actions or a few well-chosen words; they move the reader more.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The violence that accompanies sex in some novels, film, and TV is not only offensive in principle but also counterproductive. Small actions, or a few well-chosen words, can move the reader much more than an act of violence.

question: In a love between mismatched or unlikely partners, generate the reader's emotion from the conflict of repugnance slowly overcome by affection.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The interplay in the audience’s emotions may arise from the conflict of repugnance slowly overcome by affection.

question: Rewrite characterization so a character’s action — sending food back, overtipping, watching everyone — reveals background in a single stroke.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
I have a strong preference for action markers, that is sentences that describe what a character does and at the same time reveal something about the character’s upbringing or background:

Every time Zelda ate in a restaurant, she found some reason to send food back to the kitchen.

question: Use a character’s attitude — like expecting to be insulted or mugged by every passerby — as a marker of background.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote:
Attitudes can also be used as markers:

Arthur came to New York expecting to be insulted or mugged by every passerby.

question: Examine your two most important characters for social or class differences; if you have neglected such differences, add some that arouse emotion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you are presently writing a novel, have you examined it to see if there are some social or class differences between your two most important characters? How do those differences influence the story? If you have neglected such differences, how might you bolster your story by adding some social and cultural differences that arouse emotion?

question: Ask yourself what inherited trait most shaped your protagonist, what family custom haunts him, which habit he has failed to break, and what in the villain’s upbringing made him what he is — the answers supply useful markers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I have sometimes found that even accomplished writers neglect to ask themselves some fundamental questions about their important characters that could provide useful markers. For instance, what trait inherited by the protagonist has most influenced his adult life? What custom of the protagonist’s family still haunts his life? Which personal habit has he tried to break, unsuccessfully, for years? What family tradition has had the most positive influence on the protagonist? What is the single most important factor in the villain’s upbringing that contributed to his reprehensible conduct?

question: Give your main character inherited or trained baggage — upbringing, customs, temperament — and show whether they can overcome it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characters, just like people, can strive to overcome this baggage and training.

question: Delete cliché markers — the American tourist abroad hunting for hamburgers — and replace them with details that still carry surprise.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: However, be wary of cliché markers such as an American tourist abroad in search of a restaurant that serves hamburgers.

question: Use clothing to signal whether two characters belong to the same world — mismatched dress tells the reader they are not together.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Would we expect to see that woman walking in the street with a man wearing a totally sleeveless “muscle” shirt or a cap with a slogan on it? The reader assumes they are not together because they have the appurtenances of widely different backgrounds.

question: Describe a character’s clothing as a reaction to the surroundings of the scene — dress that clashes with the setting signals phoniness or contempt.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: clothing is often a reaction to the surroundings in which the clothing is worn. Keep that in mind when you’re describing a character in a specific scene.

question: Give each character markers — easily identified signals of cultural and social background — so the reader identifies their different worlds quickly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The process of identifying different worlds for the reader can be accomplished quickly through markers, easily identified signals that to the majority of readers will reveal a character’s cultural and social background.

question: Characterize instantly through public conduct — how a character behaves with children in public is an immediate marker.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Public conduct with children is an immediate marker. A woman walking with a “dressed-up” child connotes one thing. A woman screaming at her children in the supermarket suggests another.

question: Recheck your markers against today’s readers — class signifiers that once worked have diffused in time, so choose details whose connotations still register.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Though the characteristics that once connoted “lower class” and “upper class” to readers are no longer absolutes, they still work as markers in which readers find connotations and associations.

question: Run each small detail you give a character — gum chewing, an ankle bracelet, a man’s rings — past the question of what it suggests about their background.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What does the incessant chewing of gum suggest about a character? What would an ankle bracelet convey to a reader about a character? What about a man wearing multiple large rings, or a diamond ring?

question: Build the conflict of your scenes and whole plots on the cultural differences between your characters — differences are more important than similarities.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: These differences are a valuable resource for scenes as well as entire plots. It is the underlying basis of conflict in fiction.

question: Squelch your emotional reactions to your material consciously so you gain enough distance to use it in your work as a writer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer has to squelch his emotional reactions consciously in order to get enough distance to use them in his work as a writer.

question: Use what a character drinks and eats, and where, as a background marker — beer and rye versus Scotch and Perrier signal different worlds.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Food, drink, and the places they are consumed are markers. If the reader knows a character drinks popular brands of American beer, rye whiskey, and chilled red wine, what does the reader guess about the character’s background? If the character drinks Scotch, Perrier, and martinis straight up, does the reader have a different view?

question: Cut any marker that needs a paragraph of explanation — a marker should convey its point instantly or it is not working.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Distinctions of that sort are not good markers for the writer because they require too much description and readers might still not get the point without the author telling them explicitly. A marker should convey its point instantly.

question: Put two characters of sharply different backgrounds in the same story — readers’ emotions commit quickly — then step back and let the drama of their differences explode without mediating.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When in fiction, theater, and film the writer brings together people of differing social and cultural backgrounds, he needs to step back to watch the inherent drama of differences explode.

question: Cut the sentence that explains what a marker means — show only the detail, the fingernails, and let the reader draw the inference.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The writer doesn’t have to say what I’ve just said. All he has to show the reader are the fingernails; they are effective markers.

question: Characterize through how your character speaks — vocabulary, accent, verbal tics, clichés — as markers of background.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Perhaps the most frequently used marker is found in the vocabulary and expressions of a character’s dialogue.

question: Rephrase sentences that state a character’s background so the content of the character’s speech — what they know and care about — shows it instead.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Markers provide the writer with an opportunity to show the character’s background instead of telling the reader about it.

question: Discern your characters’ differences with subtlety instead of sorting them into good guys and bad guys.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In many of the films that are nominated for Academy Awards, the discernment of differences becomes more subtle. That discernment becomes a necessity in the best literary and mainstream fiction.

question: Show, in the interaction of your characters, the gap between what they profess and how they act; deal with the unspoken rather than the acceptable.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is, however, a writer’s specialty to deal with taboos, to speak the unspoken, to reveal, to uncover, to show in the interaction of people the difference between what we profess and how we act.

question: Articulate what makes your most memorable passage so good, and use that insight as a clue for what to do with your weakest part.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Consider your most memorable passage. What makes it so good? Does that provide a clue as to what you might do with your weakest part?

question: Write a metaphor by bringing together two words or phrases that do not ordinarily belong together so that their proximity conveys a fresh meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This figure of speech results when words or phrases are brought together that do not ordinarily belong together, yet by their proximity convey a fresh meaning:

question: Don’t be afraid of a long stretch in a metaphor: if it makes its point instantly, the distance between the two things is what gives it power.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It’s a long stretch from the Emperor of Japan to a light bulb, but it sure makes its point instantly.

question: Search your draft for mixed metaphors—two or more unrelated metaphors unsuccessfully combined—and rewrite one side of the image so the comparison holds together.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the hazards is, of course, the mixed metaphor, in which two or more unrelated metaphors are unsuccessfully combined:

question: Use a metaphor to set the mood of a scene: describe the setting through an image that carries the feeling you want the reader to share.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Cheever uses metaphor to set a mood: The sky was overcast, and poured down onto the dirt crossroads a very discouraging light.

question: In a nonfiction piece, find a concrete image that could carry a metaphor and add one to enhance the prose.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Metaphors can enhance nonfiction also. Witness: In some cases, generally around public buildings like the White House and State Department, the protective cordon was Saran-Wrap tight.

question: Audit the density of figures of speech in your draft: if they are overdone, they backfire—cut until each comparison earns its place.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Similes and metaphors are the wonders of writing, and like all wonderful things carry a price. If figures of speech are overdone, they backfire.

question: After cutting or changing the weakest part, find the new weakest part that has taken its place; improve it, or cut it and stitch together what comes immediately before and after.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Surprise: If you’ve cut or changed the weakest part, you have a new weakest part. In retrospect, do you know why it is weak? Can you improve it? Can you cut it and stitch together what comes immediately before and immediately after?

question: Examine the cast of your piece for two people, parties, organizations, or entities in conflict; where the conflict is not immediately apparent, bring the conflicting elements closer together and highlight it, actual or potential.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are there two people, two parties, two organizations, or two entities of any kind that are in conflict? If the conflict might not be immediately apparent to the reader, can the writer provide some help by bringing the conflicting elements closer to each other and by highlighting the conflict, actual or potential?

question: Check your article, story, or book for dramatic conflict: the reader's interest flags wherever you failed to keep in mind that dramatic conflict has been the basis of stories from the beginning of time.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In articles, newspaper stories, and books, the reader’s interest often flags because the writer did not keep in mind that dramatic conflict has been the basis of stories from the beginning of time.

question: Build and maintain suspense in your nonfiction through a consistent point of view in which the reader learns only what the narrator knows, and learns it when the narrator learns it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The following true story demonstrates how suspense can be built and maintained in nonfiction through a consistent point of view in which the reader learns only what the narrator knows, and learns it when the narrator learns it:

question: At the planning stage, consider placing your two adversaries in a crucible — a situation that holds them together more than anything drives them apart — so their conflict cannot end in a truce.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Nonfiction writing would be more dramatic and tap the reader’s emotions more if the crucible were considered more often in the planning stage.

question: Cut facts that unnecessarily diminish suspense early in your piece.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are you loading in facts that unnecessarily diminish suspense early?

question: Structure your nonfiction piece around somebody wanting something, facing obstacles, trying to get it, and finally getting or not getting it — make the conscious use of desire the engine of the telling.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: All storytelling from the beginning of recorded time is based on somebody wanting something, facing obstacles, not getting it, trying to get it, trying to overcome obstacles, and finally getting or not getting what he wanted. What has interested listeners, readers, and viewers for centuries is available in the conscious use of desire in nonfiction.

question: When preparing to write any passage or scene involving two people, focus on their differing intentions (or scripts) so their conflict positions itself in adversarial situations where conflict is inherent.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In preparing to write any passage or scene involving two people, if the writer focuses on their differing intentions (or “scripts”), he will immediately see the dramatic advantages of positioning their conflict in many kinds of adversarial situations in which conflict is inherent in the circumstances.

question: Rewrite your first paragraph so it arouses curiosity by withholding one piece of information until a bit later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Can your first paragraph arouse curiosity by withholding a piece of information till a bit later?

question: Humanize the people in your story by name and a couple of humanizing particulars before anything happens to them, particularizing as often as possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I didn’t refer to Roger as “the superintendent.” I called him by his name. I said a couple of things to humanize him. I particularized as often as possible.

question: Hold back from giving the conclusion first: starting with the outcome telegraphs the story and spoils it, even though giving the conclusion first is our instinct in life.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If I had started to recount what had happened by saying, “The superintendent of the building I was staying in burned to death last weekend,” I would have spoiled the story by telegraphing the outcome. That’s what we do in life. Our instinct is to give the conclusion first.

question: Plant the desire before the thwart: conflict can arise from a thwarted desire, but the reader must already know what was wanted for the thwarting to move them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Conflict can arise from a thwarted desire, but the desire must be planted.

question: Convert any sentence in your piece to a question that will arouse curiosity rather than satisfy it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Can you convert any sentence to a question that will arouse curiosity rather than satisfy it?

question: Raise the importance of what your subject wants: the more important the objective, the bigger the conflict will seem when obstacles block the want — even an unattainable want can stimulate the reader's emotions.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The more important the objective, the bigger the conflict will seem to the reader if there are obstacles in the way of gratifying the want. The thing that’s wanted may not be possible. Nevertheless, the reader can have his emotions stimulated by that unrealistic and unattainable want.

question: Handle the story so that at the end the reader draws his own conclusion — provide the conflict for interest but let the reader make the judgment.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This method of handling the story not only provides conflict for reader interest, at the end it lets the reader draw his own conclusion.

question: Repeat a key name or phrase deliberately — the purposeful repetition of “Mount St. Vincent” — to help set up suspense.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The purposeful repetition of “Mount St. Vincent” helps set up the suspense.

question: Separate the two parts of an action into distinct sentences — the order given, then the refusal — because the separation itself creates the tension.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What creates the tension is separating the two parts of the action.

question: Write short sentences and short paragraphs in your tense passages to increase tension, and resist the temptation to rush to a conclusion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Short sentences and short paragraphs help increase tension. A common error is the writer’s temptation to rush to a conclusion.

question: Stretch a tense situation, often a confrontation between persons or groups, out over paragraphs and pages — the continuation of tension is what keeps it alive.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The continuation of tension over paragraphs and pages comes from stretching out a tense situation, often a confrontation between persons or groups.

question: Create suspense by making the reader expect something to happen and then holding off: suspense occurs when what the reader expects is not happening yet because you are holding off.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suspense is a valuable technique for the writer who wants to make his reader keep turning pages. It occurs when the reader expects something to happen and it isn’t happening yet because the author is holding off.

question: Heighten suspense by switching to a different part of the story — another person, another thread — before the reader learns what they want to know.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The switch to a different part of the story (the spokesperson for the bus company) heightens the suspense.

question: Keep the difference between tension and suspense in mind as you build your piece: suspense arouses anxious uncertainty about what might happen, while tension involves the sudden onset of stress, strain, or pressure.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suspense arouses a feeling of anxious uncertainty in the reader about what might happen, or a hope that something bad won’t happen. Tension usually involves the sudden onset of a feeling of stress, strain, or pressure.

question: Create tension by the simple mention of a time or date that carries dread — “It was four o’clock in the morning” works because it is an hour when most people are asleep.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Tension can be created by the simple mention of a time or date. “It was four o’clock in the morning” creates tension because it’s an hour when most people are asleep.

question: Describe an action that arouses curiosity but do not explain it in the same paragraph.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you described an action that may arouse curiosity but that isn’t explained in the same paragraph?

question: Set up a question or controversy in your story and do not answer or resolve it immediately.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your story set up a question or controversy and not answer or resolve it immediately?

question: Before you begin writing, determine whether any of the people in your story want something badly, and move that material up to the beginning to touch a match to the reader's emotions.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When the writer has his material and is ready to begin writing, that’s the time to determine whether any of the people in the story he is about to write want something badly. Bringing that material up to the beginning could help touch a match to the reader’s emotions.

question: If your climax rescues the protagonist by coincidence or a deus ex machina, cut the device and find a credible way out — those devices fool no one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most dangerous place for a coincidence to occur is at the climax of a story. The protagonist has his head on the chopping block. Suddenly the deus ex machina, the god in the machine, comes down for the rescue. Those devices fool no one. They exist for the author’s convenience because he can’t figure out a credible way of rescuing the protagonist.

question: Consciously try to create stress for the reader—some delicious tension—by adapting fiction’s tension techniques to your nonfiction.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you consciously tried to create stress for the reader, some delicious tension?

question: Gain objectivity about your own work by replacing your name on a fresh title page with an admired author’s name and reading your manuscript through that author’s eyes; if that fails, use an author you dislike and go at the manuscript with a vengeance to root out unmotivated acts and coincidence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can sometimes get objectivity artificially by making a new title page and replacing your name as author with the name of an author whose work you admire especially. Then read your manuscript with that author’s eyes to see if you can catch any action that is insufficiently motivated or that smacks of coincidence. If that doesn’t work for you, try preparing a new title page and replacing your name with the name of an author whose work you dislike. Go at the manuscript with a vengeance to root out unmotivated acts and coincidence.

question: Open by personifying your subject in an incident involving an individual rather than in abstract statement.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A good way to begin is to personify your subject matter in an incident involving an individual.

question: Find the emotional root of your book in your secret snapshot and put that image on the page — start the story there, so it becomes a moving experience rather than a plot told from the outside.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In that snapshot lay the emotional root of her book. After our session, the writer started her novel with a scene in which the decoy was patting the sleeping head of her child before going off to her hazardous work. As a result, the tone of the book changed from an ordinary though suspenseful story told from the outside, to one readers could feel strongly.

question: Separate your originality into its two components—the originality of what you say and the originality of the way you say it—and clarify which one is distinctive in your current work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It usually develops over time, and has two components, the originality of what is said and the originality of the way it is said.

question: Go through a passage and examine each word for its necessity, precision, and clarity; cut or replace any word that fails one of the three.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Many authors first find their “voice” when they learn to examine each word for its necessity, precision, and clarity, as we are doing here.

question: Imagine yourself on a rooftop with the townspeople below, allowed to shout down one last sentence—the sentence the world will remember you by—and write that sentence down.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I ask you to imagine yourself on a rooftop, the townspeople assembled below. You are allowed to shout down one last sentence. It is the sentence that the world will remember you by forever.

question: Test your sentence: could any person you know have said it? Revise it until you are convinced no one else could have said that sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is your sentence one that could have been said by any person you know? If so, revise it until you are convinced no one else could have said that sentence.

question: Try making your sentence outrageous, then try turning it into a question, and compare which version is stronger.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is your sentence outrageous? Could it be? Is your sentence a question? Would it be stronger as a question?

question: Imagine the person you love most strongly disagreeing with your sentence; add a second sentence answering their disagreement, and make sure it is stronger than the first.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suppose the person you most love in all the world were to strongly disagree with your sentence. Can you answer his or her disagreement in a second sentence? Please add it. Has your second sentence weakened your first? It usually does. If so, make it stronger than the first.

question: Imagine your greatest enemy challenging your sentence; revise it so that your statement is incontrovertible and your enemy cannot take the last word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You don’t want to give your enemy the last word or let him respond in a way that would demolish what you’ve said. Can you alter your sentence so that your statement will be enemy-proof?

question: Revise your sentence so that it could be whispered and still heard, and notice whether the whisper version turns out stronger than the shouted one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suppose you found out that the only way to get your message across would be if you whispered your sentence. How would you revise it so that it would be suitable for whispering?

question: Lay out all the versions of your sentence; combine the virtues of one into another, then choose the version that is most original—the one least likely to have been written by someone else.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is there a prior version that is actually stronger than the last? Can the virtues of one be embodied in another? And most important, which sentence now strikes you as the most original, the one least likely to have been written by someone else?

question: Distrust the sentence that comes first: hone, change, and polish the words of a single sentence to test all of its possibilities.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the meantime, you’ve had another lesson in the value of shunning the sentence that comes first, and honing, changing, polishing the words of a single sentence to test all of its possibilities.

question: If you start from someone else’s secret snapshot, choose one you would never be allowed to see under any circumstance.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you elect to conjure up someone else’s secret snapshot, it has to be one that you wouldn’t be allowed to see under any circumstance.

question: Pick up the pace of a scene with a quick exchange of adversarial dialogue, letting the lines get clipped and each paragraph hold a single short sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In fiction, a quick exchange of adversarial dialogue often proves to be an ideal way of picking up pace by the use of short sentences and paragraphing.

question: When revising, find scenes that don’t work as well as you had hoped and consider skipping them entirely — if removing the scene propels the pace, you turn a liability into an asset.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In revising your manuscript, you may find some scene that doesn’t work as well as you had hoped. Consider skipping that scene and turning a liability into an asset if removing the scene propels the pace of your story.

question: Jump-cut from one scene to the next without the in-between matter of travel and transition — close the door, line space, next scene — because showing the getting-there is a drag and boring.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: With this technique, a story moves from one scene to the next without the in-between matter that would be part of getting from one place to the next.

question: Build purposeful slowdowns into your book from time to time, because readers, like athletes, must catch their breath.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Yet the best of good books have purposeful slowdowns in pace from time to time because the authors know that readers, like athletes, must catch their breath.

question: Follow each cliffhanging chapter ending with a chapter that moves to a different location or has different characters — it sustains suspense and also increases the pace of your story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the chapter on suspense, I showed how suspense can be prolonged throughout an entire book by following each cliffhanging chapter ending with a chapter that moves to a different location or has different characters.

question: Step up your pace by shortening sentences and paragraphing more frequently; the two together accelerate the pace even more than either alone.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Journalists know that short sentences step up pace. They also know that frequent paragraphing accelerates the pace. Short sentences plus frequent paragraphing step up pace even more.

question: Flip forward past a scene the reader anticipates — end the chapter before it happens and open the next elsewhere — so the scene lives only in the reader’s imagination and the pace quickens.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A technique for stepping up pace in fiction that isn’t used enough is flipping forward past a scene that never appears in the book.

question: Skip the routine steps of an action and jump from one significant beat to the next — “skipping for effect” — even if that eliminates two thirds of the words.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He washed his body, shaved his jaws, drank his coffee, and missed the seven-thirty-one. Eliminating about two thirds of the words steps up the pace brilliantly. I call this “skipping for effect.”

question: Rewrite for particularity: to be specific is not as precise as to be particular — replace the merely concrete with the particular.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Once the word from editors was “be concrete.” But to be specific is not as precise as to be particular, which is much more advantageous to the creative writer.

question: Give a character a methodical, particularized action — like moving his gaze deliberately from eyes to hair to chin to ears — that disconcerts others and reveals his nature.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thomassy moved his gaze from Roberts’s confident eyes to Roberts’s blond hair, then Roberts’s chin, then Roberts’s left ear, then Roberts’s right ear. The four points of the cross.

question: Characterize an individual through particularity — how they look, dress, or speak — without resorting to clichés or generalizations.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: To characterize, particularity is used to show how an individual looks, dresses, or speaks without resort to clichés or generalizations.

question: Audit a passage of your writing for detail that individualizes: find the particulars that differentiate one person from another, one act from another, one place from any others like it. Where the detail is generic, particularize it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is not just detail that distinguishes good writing, it is detail that individualizes. I call it “particularity.”

question: Let dialogue particularize a character: give a character a line that reveals a trait — like Joe’s "Is it in the same town?" revealing his sense of humor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In addition, the dialogue also particularizes one of the characters. Joe, for instance, has a sense of humor.

question: Go word by word through a passage and demand precision of meaning — le mot juste, exactly the right word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The requirement is precision of meaning, le mot juste, exactly the right word.

question: Convey a trait like "Vernon was a heavy smoker" through particularized evidence — how he coughs, how others treat him — rather than stating the generalization.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Vernon coughed from the ground up. When a waitress heard Vernon’s voice she always guided him to the smoking section without asking.

question: If you deal with a character's hands, give them something particular to do — like a hand that periodically checks for itself — instead of leaving them at a loss.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you’re going to deal with a character’s hands, give them something to do, as this author did:

question: Find the two most particular words in your sentence — like "bald pink knees" — and make sure the sentence would turn ordinary without them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The crucial words, of course, are “bald pink knees,” a particularization that makes the character and the place instantly visible and in the reader’s experience unique. If we were to eliminate the words “bald” and “pink” how diminished that opening sentence would be:

question: Turn an ordinary appearance sentence into one that characterizes through a measurable, comparative particular — "Cecilia’s skirts were three inches shorter than her age allowed" instead of "Cecilia wore short skirts."

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Cecilia wore short skirts. It doesn’t take much to turn that ordinariness into a sentence that characterizes and particularizes: Cecilia’s skirts were three inches shorter than her age allowed.

question: Particularize through your viewpoint character's perception: instead of saying a smile is like an implant, have the character think it is an implant.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note the use of metaphor to particularize. It doesn’t say Roberts’s smile is like an implant, Thomassy thinks it is an implant.

question: Sweep the abstractions out of your prose, for readers are attracted by particularity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt not saw the air with abstractions, for readers, like lovers, are attracted by particularity.

question: If an ordinary object matters to your story, particularize it — its location, size, color, how it moves — so the reader's attention is called to it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If an ordinary object is important to a story, particularization will help call attention to it.

question: Revise an opening that lacks particularity: use actions where possible, have people talk or think in particulars, make locale, objects, and people distinctive and visible, use other senses, and make it ominous if you can.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Use actions if possible. If people are in your opening, have them talk or think in particulars. Make locale, objects, and people distinctive and visible. Use other senses if appropriate. And make it ominous if you can.

question: Work on one paragraph at a time; perfect a single paragraph of particularity and use it as the model for the whole book.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You work on one paragraph at a time. If you perfect a single paragraph, you have a model for a book.
