question: Review every significant action for character consistency; fix any action not in keeping with the character, or that sounds farfetched, by planting a motive in a prior scene.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is there any action in your manuscript that is not in keeping with the character? Is there any action that under examination sounds farfetched? It might be fixed by planting a motive in a prior scene.

question: Read the first page as if it were written by a contemporary author you admire, then ask: is there a compelling reason to go on to page two? If not, your opening has not sparked the reader's curiosity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Now read the first page as if it were the other author's manuscript. After reading the first page, would you go on to the next page? If there isn't a compelling reason to go to page two, it usually means that you haven't sparked the reader's curiosity.

question: Read the manuscript from page one to the end as a reader and an editor, not as a writer — critically, like a tough editor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Embarking on a general revision calls for starting on page one and working through the manuscript to the end, reading as a reader and an editor, not as a writer.

question: When in doubt about a change, do not make it; note it for later consideration, and expect most of those notes to be discarded.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If in doubt about a change, don't make the change. Instead, make a note to yourself for later consideration. I find that when I look at such notes days or weeks later, many of those questionable ideas for revision get discarded.

question: Tighten the manuscript: overwriting in first drafts is normal — the skill is recognizing on a later reading what can be eliminated and having the guts to cut it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is perfectly normal to overwrite in first drafts. The test of a writer's skill is in recognizing on later reading what can be eliminated, and then having the guts to do the cutting.

question: When unsure whether a paragraph contributes, block-move it to the end of the manuscript; later, restore only the paragraphs that earn their place.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Every time he came to a paragraph he wasn't sure contributed to the book, he marked it and with a block move transferred it to the end, after the last page. When he finished he found that he had transferred dozens of paragraphs and that only one or two, in modified form, deserved a place in the text.

question: Eliminate between-the-scenes material — the offstage recounting of actions not seen — or make such material active and interesting in itself.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your second objective is to watch out for the between-the-scenes material, especially the offstage recounting of actions not seen. Try to eliminate as many of these as you can, or make them active and interesting in themselves.

question: Cut whatever seems not absolutely necessary, and watch for places where your own attention flags — that is usually a sign something needs to be revised or cut.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In your general revision, cut words, phrases, sentences, or paragraphs, pages, or whole scenes that seem not absolutely necessary. Watch for places where your own attention flags. That's usually a sign that something needs to be revised or cut.

question: Vary the length of your sentences; ideally follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt one, but avoid a mechanical short-long-short-long pattern.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your sentences are all approximately the same length, the effect will be monotonous. Vary the length of sentences. Ideally, follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt sentence. Don't do this all the time. A pattern of short-long-short-long can get almost as monotonous as all long or all short sentences.

question: Break an unbroken mellifluous cadence — a lovely rhythm, kept up, will put a reader to sleep.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An unbroken mellifluous cadence, lovely for a few sentences, if kept up will put a reader to sleep.

question: Be relentless in moving the story forward; where it bogs down and you cannot see an immediate fix, mark the place in the margin, write down what may be wrong, and come back to it later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Unless you are consciously trying to slow things down between fast-moving scenes, be relentless in moving the story forward. If you find it bogging down at any point, it could be for many reasons: perhaps too slow a pace, not enough happening. If you don't see an immediate fix, mark the place in the margin and write down what you think might be wrong.

question: Mark any section where you catch the author talking or a mix of points of view, and revise it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you catch the author talking at any point, or a mix of points of view, mark the section so that you can return to Chapter 13 for guidance.

question: Keep your characters under stress from time to time, and make the stress increase — fiction deals with the most stressful moments of the characters' lives.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are your characters under stress from time to time? Does the stress increase? Keep reminding yourself that fiction deals with the most stressful moments of the characters' lives.

question: Cut every unessential adjective and adverb; cut "very"; make every word count.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As you go through, cut every unessential adjective and adverb. Cut “very.” Cut “poor” for everything but poverty. Make every word count.

question: If you have said the same thing twice in different words, cut the weaker one; swap a repeated uncommon word for a synonym; and mark every cliché for excision.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you've said the same thing twice in different words, pick the better one and cut the other. If you find yourself using the same uncommon word twice within a few pages, use your thesaurus to pick a synonym. And in your read-through, mark every cliché for excision.

question: Put the speaker identification first ("George said") whenever there is any chance the reader will not know who is speaking; otherwise let it follow or omit it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If there is any chance that the reader won't know who is speaking at that point, the “George said” should come first. If it is clear who is speaking, “George said” can follow what he says or be omitted.

question: Transpose the order of words, phrases, or clauses in a sentence to let its emphasis fall where you want it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In my own work, I make transpositions hundreds of times in a book-length manuscript. Sometimes it is to let the emphasis of a sentence fall in a different place.

question: Transpose words when their order could make a reader momentarily misread the sentence, so the first reading is the correct one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Because readers will undoubtedly have had experience with a pulse being taken at the wrist, they may suppose that immediately on reading the word “pulse.” Immediately, they read “in the neck” and have to change their first view. That kind of glitch can momentarily disturb the reading experience. To avoid it, I simply transposed a few words.

question: Remove conspicuous passages you love — images and sentences that jump off the page and interfere with the story — and save them in a special box to look into years later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you “love” certain images or sentences, they are frequently so conspicuous as to interfere with the story. If they are, save them in a special box that you'll look into five years from now, and thank me for having asked you to remove them from your manuscript, though it may have hurt at the time.

question: Root out sentimentality — an excess of response to a stimulus — and underplay to evoke emotion in the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Root out sentimentality, which is an excess of response to a stimulus. It makes writing “flowery.” Your job is to stimulate emotions in the reader. An excessive response turns off the reader, just as it does people in life:

question: Make sure there is something visual on every page: mark V in the corner of pages that have a visual element and NV on pages that do not, then return to introduce a visual element on every NV page.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Until you are in the habit of making sure that there is something visual on every page, while reviewing the draft put a small V in the lower right corner of every page that has something visual on it. This provides a discipline as you develop the experience of reading with an editor's eye. If a page has nothing visual, mark NV and return to it later to introduce a visual element.

question: If your characters usually speak in complete sentences, fix it so they don't.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In dialogue sequences, if your characters usually speak in complete sentences, fix it so they don't.

question: Break up any dialogue that runs longer than three sentences with an interjection, thought, or action, and make responses oblique at least from time to time.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If any dialogue runs longer than three sentences, break it up with an interjection from another character or a thought or action. Check to see that responses in dialogue are oblique, at least from time to time.

question: Catch every place a character "muttered" or "screamed" instead of "said," and substitute "he said" and "she said" — the dialogue, not the tag, should tell how lines are spoken.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In your general revision, catch the places where a character “muttered,” “screamed,” and the like instead of “said.” Substitute “he said” and “she said” for language that tells the reader how the lines are spoken. That's the dialogue's job.

question: Make a checklist of everything to catch during your general revision; if you cannot do it all in one pass, save some items for a second pass.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you are new to the process, you'll want to make a checklist of all the things I've suggested catching during general revision. If you find that you just can't do everything in one pass, save some things for a second pass later on.

question: Consider whether bringing a strong scene forward would provoke the reader's curiosity more than the scene that presently starts the book.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You may want to ask yourself, if you were to bring a strong scene forward, would that provoke the reader's curiosity more than the scene that presently starts the book?

question: Make the ending of your book a high point of satisfaction for the reader; if it is not, consider whether another scene or circumstance would make a better ending.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You might consider at this stage whether the ending of your book is a high point of satisfaction for the reader. If not, is there another scene or circumstance that might make a better ending?

question: For a final read-through, work with a clean manuscript in which your changes are not visible, and fix anything that momentarily makes you see words on the page and takes you out of experiencing the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For your next read-through, work with a clean manuscript in which the changes you've made are not visible as changes. (One of the great advantages of working on a computer!) This time, as you read, watch for anything that momentarily makes you see words on the page and takes you out of experiencing the story.

question: Replace vague phrases like “a regular guy” — verbal trunks into which a hundred readers pile their own meanings — and say exactly what you mean.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did they mean Schwarzkopf was what in colloquial parlance we call “a regular guy”? And if so, what is meant by “a regular guy”? It’s a verbal trunk into which a hundred readers would pile many meanings relating to their own experience.

question: Make sure something visible appears on every page: pencil a V in the corner of each page that has something visual, and on pages without a V, create something visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is there something visible on every page? If you are reviewing what you wrote in hard copy, pencil a V in a lower corner of every page that has something visual, and on pages without a V, see if you can create something visual, even if it is a leaf falling from a tree.

question: Ask whether your opening is sufficiently visual for the reader to see it; if not, make it visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Also ask yourself if your opening is sufficiently visual to be seen by the reader.

question: Create suspense by raising a question and withholding the answer for a while; find a place in the piece where you can do this now.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you created occasional suspenseful interest by raising a question and withholding the answer for a while? Can you recall any place where this might be done now?

question: Attend to the individual meaning and resonance of every word and show respect for the reader’s intelligence — that attention is what separates literary writing from commercial.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most distinguishing difference between “commercial” writers like Grisham and literary writers is the attention paid to the individual meanings and resonance of words and the respect shown for the reader’s intelligence.

question: Bring two words together that have not been together before — achieve precision by creating a new grouping of words rather than using each word only for its exact meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One way to a reader’s emotion is to bring two words together that have not been together before. Therefore precision is achieved in poetry by the creation of a new grouping of words rather than by using each word for its exact meaning.

question: Write down what you see in your most secret snapshot — and if you’re tempted to fudge or invent one, change it to the snapshot you’re actually hiding.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the ways is to write down what you see in your most secret snapshot. If you’re tempted to fudge, don’t. If you’ve decided to give us a made-up snapshot, you’ll serve your writing better by changing it to the snapshot you’re hiding.
